paragraphs.context: She lived in one of a long row of houses
paragraphs.mainIdea: Polly sees a strange boy look over the wall. His face is very dirty, as if he had put his hands in the earth and then cried.
paragraphs.simple: Polly lived in one of a long row of houses that were all joined together. One morning she was out in the back garden. A boy climbed up from the garden next door and put his face over the wall. Polly was very surprised. Until now there had never been any children in that house. Only Mr. Ketterley and Miss Ketterley lived there. They were a brother and sister, and they were old and had never married. So Polly looked up, wanting to know more. The strange boy's face was very dirty. It could hardly have been dirtier if he had first put his hands in the earth, then cried, and then dried his face with his hands. In fact, that was very nearly what he had been doing.

paragraphs.context: But what she noticed first was a bright red wooden tray
paragraphs.mainIdea: Polly steps into the strange room. The first thing she notices is a bright red tray with rings on it, in pairs of one yellow and one green.
paragraphs.simple: The room was shaped like an attic, but it was set up as a sitting room. The walls were covered with shelves, and every shelf was full of books. A fire was burning in the fireplace, because it was a very cold, wet summer that year. In front of the fire was a high-backed armchair with its back toward the children. Between the chair and Polly was a big table that filled most of the middle of the room. It was piled with all sorts of things: printed books, books to write in, ink bottles, pens, sealing-wax and a microscope. But Polly first noticed a bright red wooden tray with a number of rings on it. They were in pairs: a yellow one and a green one together, then a little space, and then another yellow one and another green one. They were no bigger than ordinary rings, but no one could help noticing them because they were so bright. They were the most beautiful, shiny little things you can imagine. If Polly had been a very little younger, she would have wanted to put one in her mouth.

paragraphs.context: The high-backed chair in front of the fire moved suddenly
paragraphs.mainIdea: Uncle Andrew stands up from the chair in front of the fire. The children see that they are in Digory's house, in the study they must not enter.
paragraphs.simple: Digory never finished what he was going to say, because at that moment something happened. The high-backed chair in front of the fire suddenly moved, and Uncle Andrew rose up out of it, like a demon in a play coming up out of a trapdoor. It was a frightening sight. They were not in the empty house at all. They were in Digory's own house, in the study they were not allowed to enter. Both children said "O-o-oh" and knew that they had made a terrible mistake. They felt they should have known all along that they had not gone nearly far enough.

paragraphs.context: I could tell by the pricking in my fingers
paragraphs.mainIdea: Uncle Andrew tells how his godmother gave him a secret box. She made him promise to burn it unopened, but he did not keep the promise.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Andrew said that they let old Mrs. Lefay out before she died. He was one of the very few people she would let see her when she was ill. By then she disliked ordinary, ignorant people, and so did he. But she and he were interested in the same sort of things. Only a few days before she died, she told him to go to an old desk in her house, open a secret drawer, and bring her a little box that he would find there. The moment he picked up the box, he felt a pricking in his fingers and knew that he held some great secret. She gave it to him. She made him promise that as soon as she was dead, he would burn it, unopened, with certain ceremonies. He did not keep that promise.

paragraphs.context: rules of that sort, however excellent they may be for little boys
paragraphs.mainIdea: Uncle Andrew says that rules, such as keeping promises, are not for great thinkers like him. He says men like him are free from common rules.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Andrew looked puzzled and said, "Rotten?" Then he said that he understood. Little boys ought to keep their promises. That was right and proper, and he was glad Digory had been taught to do it. But he said that Digory must understand that rules of that sort cannot be expected to apply to deep students, great thinkers and wise men. The rules may be excellent for little boys, servants, women and even people in general. Men like him, who have hidden wisdom, are free from common rules, just as they are cut off from the pleasures of ordinary people. He said, "Ours, my boy, is a high and lonely destiny."

paragraphs.context: It was the quietest wood you could possibly imagine
paragraphs.mainIdea: Digory finds himself in a very quiet wood with many pools. The wood feels very much alive.
paragraphs.simple: Digory stood up. He was not dripping and not out of breath, though you would expect that after being under water. His clothes were perfectly dry. He was standing by the edge of a small pool, not more than ten feet from side to side, in a wood. The trees grew close together and had so many leaves that he could not see the sky. All the light was green light that came through the leaves. It was bright and warm, so there must have been a very strong sun overhead. It was the quietest wood you could imagine. There were no birds, no insects, no animals and no wind. You could almost feel the trees growing. The pool he had just got out of was not the only pool. There were dozens of others, a pool every few yards as far as he could see. You could almost feel the trees drinking the water up with their roots. This wood was very much alive. When Digory tried to describe it afterward, he always said, "It was a rich place: as rich as plumcake."
hardWords: as far as his eyes could reach

paragraphs.context: Both the men and women looked kind and wise
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children walk past the stone figures in the room. The faces change from kind to cruel, and the last is a very tall, proud, beautiful woman.
paragraphs.simple: Polly nodded. All the faces they could see were nice. The men and women looked kind and wise, and they seemed to come from a good-looking family. But after the children had gone a few steps down the room, they came to faces that looked a little different. These were very serious faces. You felt you would have to be very careful how you behaved if you ever met living people who looked like that. Further on, about the middle of the room, they found faces they did not like. These faces looked strong and proud and happy, but they looked cruel. A little further on they looked crueler. Further on again, they were still cruel, but they no longer looked happy. They were even faces without hope, as if the people had done terrible things and had also suffered terrible things. The last figure of all was the most interesting. It was a woman even more richly dressed than the others, and very tall (but every figure in that room was taller than the people of our world). She looked so fierce and proud that it took your breath away. But she was beautiful too. Years afterward, when he was an old man, Digory said he had never in all his life known a woman so beautiful. Polly always said she could not see anything specially beautiful about her.

paragraphs.context: he grabbed her wrist, leaning across her with his back
paragraphs.mainIdea: Digory stops Polly from using her ring to leave, and he hits the golden bell. He is very sorry for it afterward.
paragraphs.simple: Digory said "None of that!" in a voice even nastier than he meant it to be, because he saw Polly's hand moving to her pocket to get hold of her yellow ring. The writer says that he cannot excuse what Digory did next, except to say that Digory was very sorry for it afterward (and so were a good many other people). Before Polly's hand reached her pocket, Digory took hold of her wrist, leaning across her with his back against her chest. He kept her other arm out of the way with his other elbow. Then he leaned forward, picked up the hammer and gave the golden bell a light, quick tap. Then he let her go. They fell apart, staring at each other and breathing hard. Polly was just beginning to cry. It was not from fear, and not even because he had hurt her wrist quite badly, but from furious anger. Within two seconds, however, they had something to think about that drove their quarrels right out of their minds.

paragraphs.context: there was a word which, if spoken with the proper ceremonies
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jadis tells about a secret word that would destroy every living thing except the one who said it. She learned it in a secret place and paid a terrible price.
paragraphs.simple: Jadis said that the great kings of her family had long known about a word. If a person said it with the right ceremonies, it would destroy all living things except the one who said it. But the old kings were weak and soft-hearted. They and all the kings after them made great promises never even to try to learn that word. But Jadis learned it in a secret place and paid a terrible price to learn it. She did not use it until her sister forced her to. She fought to win by every other way first. She poured out the blood of her armies like water.

paragraphs.context: I did not use my power till the last of my soldiers
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jadis tells how she said the Deplorable Word when her sister's army came close. After that, she was the only living thing left.
paragraphs.simple: Jadis said that the last great battle went on for three days in Charn itself. For those three days she looked down on it from the same place. She did not use her power until the last of her soldiers had fallen. Her sister, the cursed woman, was at the head of her rebels, halfway up the great stairs that lead from the city to the terrace. Then Jadis waited until they were so close that they could see each other's faces. Her sister looked at her with horrible, wicked eyes and said, "Victory." Jadis said, "Yes, Victory, but not yours." Then she said the Deplorable Word. A moment later she was the only living thing under the sun.

paragraphs.context: it is enough if you are touching someone who is touching it
paragraphs.mainIdea: A person who touches someone who is touching a ring also goes to the other world. The rings work like a magnet.
paragraphs.simple: This showed another thing about the rings. Uncle Andrew had not told Digory, because he did not know it himself. To jump from world to world with one of those rings, you do not need to wear it or touch it yourself. It is enough if you are touching someone who is touching it. In that way the rings work like a magnet. Everyone knows that if you pick up a pin with a magnet, any other pin that is touching the first pin will come too.

paragraphs.context: she fairly took one’s breath away
paragraphs.mainIdea: In London, Jadis looks even more frightening than in Charn. She is very big, and Uncle Andrew seems small beside her.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Andrew stared, and well he might. Digory and Polly stared too. The Witch was no longer faint. Now they saw her in our own world, with ordinary things around her, and she took their breath away. In Charn she had been frightening enough, but in London she was terrifying. Until now they had not seen how very big she was. Digory thought, "Hardly human." He may have been right, because some say there is the blood of giants in the royal family of Charn. But even her height was nothing compared with her beauty, her fierceness and her wildness. She looked ten times more alive than most of the people one meets in London. Uncle Andrew was bowing and rubbing his hands and looking extremely frightened. He seemed a very small creature beside the Witch. Yet, as Polly said afterward, there was a sort of likeness between her face and his, something in the look on it. It was the look that all wicked Magicians have, the "Mark" that Jadis had said she could not find in Digory's face. One good thing about seeing the two together was that you would never again be afraid of Uncle Andrew. You would not be afraid of a worm after you had met a rattlesnake, or of a cow after you had met a mad bull.

paragraphs.context: swaying with superb balance as it came at full speed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jadis comes back standing on the roof of a cab, beating the horse. The cab crashes into the lamp-post, and she jumps onto the horse's back.
paragraphs.simple: First came the hansom (a horse cab). There was no one in the driver's seat. Jadis, the Queen of Queens and the Terror of Charn, was standing on the roof, not sitting. She kept her balance very well as it came round the corner at full speed with one wheel in the air. Her teeth showed, her eyes shone like fire, and her long hair streamed out behind her like the tail of a comet. She was beating the horse without mercy. Its nostrils were wide and red, and its sides were spotted with foam. It galloped madly up to the front door, missing the lamp-post by an inch, and then rose up on its back legs. The cab crashed into the lamp-post and broke into several pieces. With a magnificent jump, the Witch had sprung clear just in time and landed on the horse's back. She sat with a leg on each side and leaned forward, whispering things in its ear. They must have been things meant not to make it quiet but to make it wild. In a moment it was on its back legs again, and its cry was like a scream. It was all hoofs and teeth and eyes and tossing mane. Only a splendid rider could have stayed on its back.

paragraphs.context: the blackness overhead, all at once, was blazing with stars
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the dark, many high voices join the first deep voice, and stars appear at the same moment. Digory feels sure that the stars are singing.
paragraphs.simple: Then two wonders happened at the same moment. One was that other voices suddenly joined the first voice, more voices than you could count. They sang with it, but far higher: cold, tingling, silvery voices. The second wonder was that the blackness overhead was suddenly full of bright stars. They did not come out gently one by one, as they do on a summer evening. One moment there was nothing but darkness. The next moment a thousand, thousand points of light jumped out: single stars, groups of stars and planets, brighter and bigger than any in our world. There were no clouds. The new stars and the new voices began at exactly the same time. If you had seen and heard it as Digory did, you would have been quite sure that the stars themselves were singing, and that the first voice, the deep one, had made them appear and made them sing.

paragraphs.context: And as he walked and sang the valley grew green with grass
paragraphs.mainIdea: As Aslan sings a new song, grass and then trees grow across the land. Digory watches the trees grow.
paragraphs.simple: The Lion was walking to and fro in that empty land, singing his new song. It was softer than the song that had called up the stars and the sun. It was a gentle, rippling music. As he walked and sang, the valley turned green with grass. The green spread out from the Lion like a pool. It ran up the sides of the little hills like a wave. In a few minutes it was creeping up the lower slopes of the faraway mountains, making that young world softer every moment. Now the light wind could be heard moving the grass. Soon there were other things besides grass. The higher slopes grew dark with heather. Patches of rougher green appeared in the valley. Digory did not know what they were until one began coming up very close to him. It was a little, spiky thing that put out dozens of arms and covered them with green. It grew about an inch every two seconds. There were dozens of these things all round him now. When they were nearly as tall as he was, he saw what they were. "Trees!" he said.

paragraphs.context: every now and then he would go up to two of them
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan goes among the animals and touches two at a time on the nose. The chosen animals stand in a circle round him, in complete silence.
paragraphs.simple: Digory could no longer hear the Lion, but he could see it. It was so big and bright that he could not take his eyes off it. The other animals did not seem afraid of it. Then Digory heard the sound of hoofs behind him, and the old cab-horse trotted past and joined the other beasts. (The air seemed to have been as good for him as for Uncle Andrew. He no longer looked like the poor old slave he had been in London. He was lifting his feet and holding his head up.) For the first time the Lion was quite silent. He went to and fro among the animals. Every now and then he would go up to two of them, always two at a time, and touch their noses with his own. He touched two beavers among all the beavers, two leopards among all the leopards, and one stag and one deer among all the deer, and he left the rest. Some kinds of animal he passed by altogether. But the pairs he had touched at once left their own kind and followed him. At last he stood still, and all the animals he had touched came and stood in a wide circle around him. The others began to wander away. The chosen animals who stayed were completely silent, with their eyes fixed on the Lion. The cat-like ones gave an occasional twitch of the tail, but otherwise all were still. For the first time that day there was complete silence, except for the noise of running water. Digory's heart beat wildly. He knew that something very serious was going to be done. He had not forgotten his Mother, but he knew that even for her he could not interrupt a thing like this.

paragraphs.context: I give to you forever this land of Narnia
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan gives the land of Narnia and everything in it to the creatures. He tells them not to go back to the ways of the Dumb Beasts, or they will stop being Talking Beasts.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan said in his strong, happy voice, "Creatures, I give you yourselves. I give you this land of Narnia for ever. I give you the woods, the fruits and the rivers. I give you the stars, and I give you myself. The Dumb Beasts that I have not chosen are yours too. Be gentle with them and take care of them. But do not go back to their ways, or you will stop being Talking Beasts. You were taken out of them, and you can go back into them. Do not do so."

paragraphs.context: is seven hours old, a force of evil has already entered it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan says that a force of evil has already come into his new world, brought by Digory. People of Adam's race must help to put right the harm.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan said, "You see, friends, that before the new, clean world I gave you is seven hours old, a force of evil has already come into it. This Son of Adam woke it and brought it here." All the Beasts, even Strawberry, looked at Digory until he wished the ground would swallow him up. "But do not be sad," Aslan said to the Beasts. "Evil will come of that evil, but it is still a long way off, and I will see to it that the worst falls on me. In the meantime, let us put things in order, so that for many hundred years this will be a happy land in a happy world. Adam's race has done the harm, so Adam's race will help to heal it. Come near, you other two."

paragraphs.context: It is my wish to plant in Narnia a tree
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan says the Witch will come back to Narnia, but not yet. He wants a tree that she will not dare to come near, and Digory must bring the seed for it.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan said, "My son, my son, I know. Grief is great. Only you and I in this land know that yet. Let us be good to one another. But I have to think of hundreds of years in the life of Narnia. The Witch whom you have brought into this world will come back to Narnia again. But it need not be yet. I want to plant in Narnia a tree that she will not dare to come near. That tree will keep Narnia safe from her for many years. So this land will have a long, bright morning before any clouds come over the sun. You must get me the seed from which that tree is to grow."

paragraphs.context: there burst out from the shoulders of Fledge wings that spread
paragraphs.mainIdea: Wings burst out from Fledge's shoulders. He flies up, goes round once, and comes down looking awkward and surprised but extremely pleased.
paragraphs.simple: Then, just as the animals had burst out of the earth, wings burst out from the shoulders of Fledge. They spread and grew, bigger than the wings of eagles, bigger than the wings of swans, and bigger than angels' wings in church windows. The feathers shone chestnut color and copper color. He gave a great sweep with them and jumped into the air. Twenty feet above Aslan and Digory, he snorted, neighed and made little jumps in the air. Then he went round once and dropped to the earth, all four hoofs together. He looked awkward and surprised, but extremely pleased.

paragraphs.context: A terrible thirst and hunger came over him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Digory badly wants to taste the apple and begins to think it might not be wrong. He has already taken one "for others".
paragraphs.simple: It would have been better if Digory had not looked at the apple and smelled it. A terrible thirst and hunger came over him, and a longing to taste that fruit. He quickly put it into his pocket, but there were plenty of others. Could it be wrong to taste one? After all, he thought, the notice on the gate might not have been exactly an order. It might have been only a piece of advice, and who cares about advice? Or even if it was an order, would he be breaking it by eating an apple? He had already done what it said about taking one "for others."

paragraphs.context: There, only a few yards away from him, stood the Witch
paragraphs.mainIdea: Digory finds the Witch in the garden. She has eaten an apple, and she looks stronger and prouder, but her face is deadly white.
paragraphs.simple: Digory was just turning to go back to the gates when he stopped to have one last look round. He got a terrible shock. He was not alone. Only a few yards away from him stood the Witch. She was just throwing away the core of an apple that she had eaten. The juice was darker than you would expect and had made a horrible stain round her mouth. Digory guessed at once that she must have climbed in over the wall. He began to see that there might be some sense in that last line about getting your heart's desire and getting despair along with it. The Witch looked stronger and prouder than ever, and even, in a way, like a winner. But her face was deadly white, as white as salt.

paragraphs.context: one bite of that apple would heal her
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Witch tells Digory to take the apple to his Mother. She says it would make her well and that his home would be happy again.
paragraphs.simple: The Witch said, "Do you not see, Fool, that one bite of that apple would make her well? You have it in your pocket. We are here by ourselves, and the Lion is far away. Use your Magic and go back to your own world. A minute later you can be at your Mother's bedside, giving her the fruit. Five minutes later you will see the color coming back to her face. She will tell you the pain is gone. Soon she will tell you she feels stronger. Then she will fall asleep. Think of that: hours of sweet, natural sleep, without pain, without drugs. Next day everyone will be saying how well she has got. Soon she will be quite well again. All will be well again. Your home will be happy again. You will be like other boys."

paragraphs.context: let it be your first care to guard this Tree
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan tells the Narnians to guard the Tree. While it grows well, the Witch will not come near it, because its smell is death and horror to her.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan said, "Son of Adam, you have sown well. And you, Narnians, make it your first care to guard this Tree, for it is your Shield. The Witch of whom I told you has run far away into the North of the world. She will live on there, growing stronger in dark Magic. But while that tree grows well, she will never come down into Narnia. She dare not come within a hundred miles of the Tree, for its smell, which is joy and life and health to you, is death and horror and despair to her."

paragraphs.context: Things always work according to their nature
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan says that the fruit does work for the Witch: she has strength and endless days. But a long life with an evil heart is only a long misery.
paragraphs.simple: "Alas," said Aslan, and he shook his head. "It will. Things always work according to their nature. She has won her heart's desire. She has strength that never tires and endless days, like a goddess. But a long life with an evil heart is only a long misery, and already she begins to know it. All get what they want; they do not always like it."

paragraphs.context: great nations in your world will be ruled by tyrants
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan says that the children's world is growing more like Charn. He warns that tyrants will rule great nations, and he tells the children to bury the magic rings.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan said, "Not yet, Daughter of Eve. But you are growing more like it. It is not certain that some wicked one of your race will not find out a secret as evil as the Deplorable Word and use it to destroy all living things. And very soon, before you are an old man and an old woman, great nations in your world will be ruled by tyrants. They will care no more for joy and justice and mercy than the Empress Jadis. Let your world beware. That is the warning. Now for the command. As soon as you can, take from your Uncle his magic rings and bury them, so that no one can use them again."

paragraphs.context: a real, natural, gentle sleep, without any of those nasty drugs
paragraphs.mainIdea: Digory's Mother eats the apple and falls into a real, natural sleep. Digory thinks her face looks different, and he begins to hope.
paragraphs.simple: Digory peeled the apple, cut it up and gave it to his Mother piece by piece. As soon as she had finished it, she smiled, her head went back on the pillow, and she was asleep. It was a real, natural, gentle sleep, without any of those nasty drugs. Digory knew that this was the thing she wanted most in the whole world. He was sure now that her face looked a little different. He bent down and kissed her very softly and went quietly out of the room with a beating heart, taking the core of the apple with him. For the rest of that day, when he looked at the things around him and saw how ordinary they were, with no magic in them, he hardly dared to hope. But when he remembered the face of Aslan, he did hope.

paragraphs.context: That was the beginning of all the comings and goings between Narnia and our world
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree that grew from the apple core in England had apples that were not fully magical. A storm blew it down, and Digory had a wardrobe made from its wood. That began the comings and goings between Narnia and our world.
paragraphs.simple: The tree that grew from the core of the Apple that Digory planted in the back garden grew into a fine tree. It grew in the soil of our world, far from the sound of Aslan's voice and far from the young air of Narnia. So it did not bear apples that could bring a dying woman back to health, as Digory's Mother had been. It did bear apples more beautiful than any others in England, and they were extremely good for you, though not fully magical. But inside itself, in its sap, the tree never forgot that other tree in Narnia. Sometimes it would move when there was no wind. The writer thinks this happened when there were high winds in Narnia, and the English tree shook because the Narnia tree was rocking in a strong southwestern gale. Later it was proved that there was still magic in its wood. When Digory was quite middle-aged, a famous learned man, a Professor and a great traveler, the old house of the Ketterleys belonged to him. Then a great storm all over the south of England blew the tree down. He could not bear to have it simply chopped up for firewood, so he had part of the wood made into a wardrobe, which he put in his big house in the country. He did not find the magic of that wardrobe himself, but someone else did. That was the beginning of all the comings and goings between Narnia and our world, which you can read about in other books.

paragraphs.context: sent away from London during the war because of the air-raids
paragraphs.mainIdea: Four children are sent from London to an old Professor's big house in the country. Lucy is a little afraid of him, and Edmund wants to laugh.
paragraphs.simple: Once there were four children called Peter, Susan, Edmund and Lucy. This story is about something that happened to them when they were sent away from London during the war because of the air raids. They were sent to the house of an old Professor. He lived in the heart of the country, ten miles from the nearest railway station and two miles from the nearest post office. He had no wife, and he lived in a very large house with a housekeeper called Mrs Macready and three servants. (Their names were Ivy, Margaret and Betty, but they do not come into the story much.) He was a very old man with shaggy white hair, which grew over most of his face as well as on his head. The children liked him almost at once. But on the first evening, when he came out to meet them at the front door, he looked so odd that Lucy, who was the youngest, was a little afraid of him. Edmund, who was the next youngest, wanted to laugh. He had to keep on pretending that he was blowing his nose, to hide it.
hardWords: in the heart of the country

paragraphs.context: She immediately stepped into the wardrobe and got in among the coats
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lucy goes into the wardrobe and walks in among the coats. She goes further and further in, but she cannot feel the back of the wardrobe.
paragraphs.simple: Inside the wardrobe, Lucy saw several coats hanging up, mostly long fur coats. There was nothing Lucy liked so much as the smell and feel of fur. She stepped into the wardrobe at once, got in among the coats and rubbed her face against them. She left the door open, of course, because she knew that it is very foolish to shut yourself into any wardrobe. Soon she went further in and found a second row of coats hanging up behind the first one. It was almost quite dark in there. She kept her arms stretched out in front of her, so as not to bump her face into the back of the wardrobe. She took a step further in, then two or three steps, always expecting to feel wood against the tips of her fingers. But she could not feel it.

paragraphs.context: From the waist upward he was like a man, but his legs were
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the snow, Lucy sees a very strange person. He is half man and half goat, and he is a Faun.
paragraphs.simple: He was only a little taller than Lucy herself. Over his head he carried an umbrella that was white with snow. From the waist up he was like a man. But his legs were shaped like a goat's, and the hair on them was shiny black. Instead of feet he had goat's hoofs. He also had a tail, but Lucy did not see this at first. It was neatly caught up over the arm that held the umbrella, so that it would not trail in the snow. He had a red wool scarf round his neck, and his skin was rather red too. He had a strange but pleasant little face, with a short pointed beard and curly hair. Out of the hair stuck two horns, one on each side of his forehead. One of his hands held the umbrella. In his other arm he carried several brown-paper parcels. With the parcels and the snow, it looked just as if he had been doing his Christmas shopping. He was a Faun. When he saw Lucy, he gave such a start of surprise that he dropped all his parcels.

paragraphs.context: I’m a kidnapper for her, that’s what I am.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Tumnus says he is a kidnapper for the White Witch. He asks if Lucy would believe that he would pretend to be friendly to a child and then hand it over to the Witch.
paragraphs.simple: "That is the worst of it," said Mr. Tumnus with a deep groan. "I am a kidnapper for her. That is what I am. Look at me, Daughter of Eve. Would you believe that I am the sort of Faun who would meet a poor innocent child in the wood, one that had never done me any harm, and pretend to be friendly with it, and invite it home to my cave, all for the sake of making it fall asleep and then handing it over to the White Witch?"

paragraphs.context: she’ll wave her wand over my beautiful cloven hoofs
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Tumnus says that if he does not do it, the Witch will find out and hurt him. She may even turn him into stone.
paragraphs.simple: "And if I don't," he said, beginning to cry again, "she is sure to find out. She will have my tail cut off, and my horns sawn off, and my beard pulled out. She will wave her wand over my beautiful hoofs, which are split in two, and turn them into horrid solid hoofs like a horse's. And if she is extra and specially angry, she will turn me into stone. I shall be only a statue of a Faun in her horrible house, until the four thrones at Cair Paravel are filled. And goodness knows when that will happen, or whether it will ever happen at all."

paragraphs.context: He jumped in and shut the door, forgetting what a very foolish thing
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmund follows Lucy into the wardrobe to go on teasing her. He shuts the door and then cannot find it.
paragraphs.simple: The steps Lucy had heard were those of Edmund. He came into the room just in time to see Lucy vanishing into the wardrobe. At once he decided to get into it himself. He did not think it was a particularly good place to hide. He wanted to go on teasing her about her imaginary country. He opened the door. The coats were hanging up as usual, and there was a smell of moth-balls, and darkness and silence, and no sign of Lucy. "She thinks I am Susan come to catch her," said Edmund to himself, "and so she is keeping very quiet in at the back." He jumped in and shut the door, forgetting what a very foolish thing this is to do. Then he began feeling about for Lucy in the dark. He had expected to find her in a few seconds, and he was very surprised when he did not. He decided to open the door again and let in some light. But he could not find the door either. He did not like this at all, and he began groping wildly in every direction. He even shouted out, "Lucy! Lu! Where are you? I know you are here."

paragraphs.context: he is only one, and he is easily dealt with
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Queen hears that Edmund came through a door from the world of men. Edmund feels sure that she will do something dreadful, but then she seems to change her mind.
paragraphs.simple: "Ha!" said the Queen, speaking more to herself than to him. "A door. A door from the world of men! I have heard of such things. This may spoil everything. But he is only one, and he is easy to deal with." As she said these words, she stood up from her seat and looked Edmund full in the face. Her eyes were flaming. At the same moment she raised her wand. Edmund felt sure that she was going to do something dreadful, but he seemed unable to move. Then, just as he gave himself up for lost, she seemed to change her mind.

The Queen probably knew quite well what he was thinking. She knew, though Edmund did not, that this was enchanted Turkish Delight. She knew that anyone who had once tasted it would want more and more of it. If they were allowed, they would even go on eating it until they killed themselves. But she did not offer him any more. Instead, she said to him,

paragraphs.context: the other world had a separate time of its own
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Professor says Lucy's story may be true. Another world could have its own time.
paragraphs.simple: "That is the very thing that makes her story so likely to be true," said the Professor. "If there really is a door in this house that leads to some other world (and I should warn you that this is a very strange house, and even I know very little about it), and if she had got into another world, I should not be at all surprised to find that the other world had a separate time of its own. So however long you stayed there, it would never take up any of our time. On the other hand, I do not think many girls of her age would invent that idea for themselves. If she had been pretending, she would have hidden for a reasonable time before coming out and telling her story."

paragraphs.context: is under arrest and awaiting his trial on a charge of High Treason
paragraphs.mainIdea: A notice says that the Faun Tumnus is under arrest and waiting for his trial. It names the charges against him.
paragraphs.simple: The notice says: The Faun Tumnus, who used to live in this place, is under arrest. He is waiting for his trial. He is charged with High Treason against her Imperial Majesty Jadis, Queen of Narnia, Chatelaine of Cair Paravel, Empress of the Lone Islands, and so on. He is also charged with comforting her said Majesty's enemies, hiding spies and being friendly with Humans.

paragraphs.context: None of the children knew who Aslan was any more than you do
paragraphs.mainIdea: When the Beaver says the name of Aslan, each child feels something strong, and each feels it in a different way. The writer compares it to a dream with a very big meaning.
paragraphs.simple: And now a very strange thing happened. None of the children knew who Aslan was, any more than you do. But the moment the Beaver had said these words, everyone felt quite different. Perhaps in a dream someone has said something to you that you did not understand, but in the dream it felt as if it had some enormous meaning. It may be a terrible meaning that turns the whole dream into a nightmare. Or it may be a lovely meaning, too lovely to put into words, which makes the dream so beautiful that you remember it all your life and are always wishing you could get into that dream again. It was like that now. At the name of Aslan, each one of the children felt something jump inside. Edmund felt a feeling of mysterious horror. Peter suddenly felt brave and ready for adventure. Susan felt as if a lovely smell or some lovely music had just floated by her. And Lucy got the feeling you have when you wake up in the morning and know that it is the beginning of the holidays or the beginning of summer.

paragraphs.context: a saying in Narnia time out of mind that when two Sons of Adam
paragraphs.mainIdea: An old saying in Narnia says that when two Sons of Adam and two Daughters of Eve sit on the four thrones at Cair Paravel, the Witch's rule and her life will end.
paragraphs.simple: "Because of another prophecy," said Mr. Beaver. "Down at Cair Paravel there are four thrones. That is the castle on the seacoast, down at the mouth of this river. It ought to be the capital of the whole country, if all was as it should be. It is a saying in Narnia, from time out of mind, that when two Sons of Adam and two Daughters of Eve sit on those four thrones, it will be the end not only of the White Witch's reign but of her life. That is why we had to be so careful as we came along. If she knew about you four, your lives would not be worth a shake of my whiskers!"
hardWords: wouldn’t be worth a shake of my whiskers

paragraphs.context: he has already met the White Witch and joined her side
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Beaver says that Edmund has already met the White Witch and joined her side. He says he could tell by Edmund's look.
paragraphs.simple: "Then mark my words," said Mr. Beaver. "He has already met the White Witch and joined her side, and been told where she lives. I did not like to mention it before, because he is your brother. But the moment I set eyes on that brother of yours, I said to myself, 'Treacherous.' He had the look of one who has been with the Witch and eaten her food. You can always tell them if you have lived long in Narnia. There is something about their eyes."

paragraphs.context: Edmund crept up to the arch and looked inside into the courtyard
paragraphs.mainIdea: At the Witch's house, Edmund sees an enormous lion crouching in the courtyard. He is afraid to go on and afraid to go back.
paragraphs.simple: Edmund crept up to the arch and looked inside into the courtyard. There he saw a sight that nearly made his heart stop beating. Just inside the gate, with the moonlight shining on it, stood an enormous lion, crouched as if it was ready to spring. Edmund stood in the shadow of the arch. He was afraid to go on and afraid to go back, and his knees were knocking together. He stood there so long that his teeth would have been chattering with cold, even if they had not been chattering with fear. The writer says, "How long this really lasted I don't know," but it seemed to Edmund to last for hours.

paragraphs.context: He took a stump of lead pencil out of his pocket
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmund thinks the stone lion is Aslan. He draws on its face to laugh at it, but its face still looks terrible, sad and noble.
paragraphs.simple: And he stood there enjoying the sight of the stone lion, and presently he did something very silly and childish. He took a stump of lead pencil out of his pocket and scribbled a mustache on the lion's upper lip and then a pair of spectacles on its eyes. Then he said, "Yah! Silly old Aslan! How do you like being a stone? You thought yourself mighty fine, didn't you?" But in spite of the scribbles on it, the face of the great stone beast still looked so terrible, and sad, and noble, staring up in the moonlight, that Edmund did not really get any fun out of jeering at it. He turned away and began to cross the courtyard.

paragraphs.context: he handed to Peter a shield and a sword
paragraphs.mainIdea: Father Christmas gives Peter a shield and a sword. He says they are tools, not toys.
paragraphs.simple: "These are your presents," was the answer, "and they are tools, not toys. The time to use them is perhaps near. Bear them well." With these words he handed Peter a shield and a sword. The shield was the color of silver, and across it there was a red lion standing up on its back legs, as bright as a ripe strawberry at the moment when you pick it. The handle of the sword was gold. It had a sheath and a sword belt and everything it needed, and it was just the right size and weight for Peter to use. Peter was silent and serious as he received these gifts, because he felt they were a very serious kind of present.

paragraphs.context: she had waved her wand and instantly where the merry party had been
paragraphs.mainIdea: A young squirrel cries out that Father Christmas has been there. The Witch waves her wand and turns the whole happy party into stone.
paragraphs.simple: "He has, he has, he has!" it squeaked, beating its little spoon on the table. Edmund saw the Witch bite her lips so that a drop of blood showed on her white cheek. Then she raised her wand. "Oh, don't, don't, please don't," shouted Edmund. But even while he was shouting, she waved her wand. At once, where the happy party had been, there were only statues of creatures. One had its stone fork stuck forever halfway to its stone mouth. They were sitting round a stone table, on which there were stone plates and a stone plum pudding.

paragraphs.context: didn’t know what to do or say when they saw him
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children meet Aslan. He is good and terrible at the same time, and they cannot look at his face for long.
paragraphs.simple: As for Aslan himself, the Beavers and the children did not know what to do or say when they saw him. People who have not been in Narnia sometimes think that a thing cannot be good and terrible at the same time. If the children had ever thought so, they were cured of it now. When they tried to look at Aslan's face, they just caught a glimpse of the golden mane and the great, royal, serious, overwhelming eyes. Then they found they could not look at him, and they went all trembly.

paragraphs.context: He rushed straight up to the monster and aimed a slash of his sword
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter does not feel brave, but he runs at the Wolf and kills it with his sword. Afterwards he feels tired all over.
paragraphs.simple: Peter did not feel very brave. Indeed, he felt he was going to be sick. But that made no difference to what he had to do. He rushed straight up to the monster and aimed a slash of his sword at its side. That stroke never reached the Wolf. Quick as lightning it turned round, its eyes flaming and its mouth wide open in a howl of anger. If it had not been so angry that it simply had to howl, it would have got him by the throat at once. As it was, he had just time to duck down and push his sword, as hard as he could, between the brute's forelegs into its heart. All this happened too quickly for Peter to think at all. Then came a horrible, confused moment like something in a nightmare. He was tugging and pulling. The Wolf seemed neither alive nor dead. Its bared teeth knocked against his forehead, and everything was blood and heat and hair. A moment later he found that the monster lay dead, and he had drawn his sword out of it. He was straightening his back and rubbing the sweat off his face and out of his eyes. He felt tired all over.

paragraphs.context: your master can rob me of my rights by mere force
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Witch says Aslan cannot take her rights by force. By the Law, she must have blood, or Narnia will be lost.
paragraphs.simple: "Fool," said the Witch with a wild smile that was almost a snarl, "do you really think your master can rob me of my rights by mere force? He knows the Deep Magic better than that. He knows that unless I have blood, as the Law says, all Narnia will be overturned and will be lost in fire and water."

paragraphs.context: Ogres with monstrous teeth, and wolves, and bull-headed men
paragraphs.mainIdea: A great crowd of the Witch's side stands round the Stone Table, many with torches. The Witch herself is in the middle.
paragraphs.simple: A great crowd of people were standing all round the Stone Table. The moon was shining, but many of them carried torches. The torches burned with evil-looking red flames and black smoke. But such people! There were ogres with monstrous teeth, and wolves, and men with bulls' heads. There were spirits of evil trees and poisonous plants. There were other creatures whom the writer will not describe, because the grown-ups would probably not let you read this book if he did. They were Cruels, Hags, Incubuses, Wraiths, Horrors, Efreets, Sprites, Orknies, Wooses and Ettins. In fact, here were all those who were on the Witch's side and whom the Wolf had called together at her command. And right in the middle, standing by the Table, was the Witch herself.

paragraphs.context: Now I will kill you instead of him as our pact was
paragraphs.mainIdea: Before she kills Aslan, the Witch says that he has given her Narnia and has not saved Edmund. She tells him to despair and die.
paragraphs.simple: "And now, who has won? Fool, did you think that by all this you would save the human traitor? Now I will kill you instead of him, as our pact was, and so the Deep Magic will be satisfied. But when you are dead, what will stop me from killing him as well? And who will take him out of my hand then? Understand that you have given me Narnia forever. You have lost your own life, and you have not saved his. In that knowledge, despair and die."

paragraphs.context: there is a magic deeper still which she did not know
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan tells why he is alive. There is a magic deeper than the Deep Magic, and the Witch did not know it.
paragraphs.simple: "It means," said Aslan, "that though the Witch knew the Deep Magic, there is a magic deeper still which she did not know. Her knowledge goes back only to the dawn of time. But if she could have looked a little further back, into the stillness and the darkness before Time dawned, she would have read there a different spell. She would have known that when a willing victim who had done no treachery was killed in a traitor's place, the Table would crack and Death itself would start working backward. And now--"

paragraphs.context: I expect you’ve seen someone put a lighted match to a bit of newspaper
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer compares the stone lion coming to life to a small flame spreading over a piece of newspaper.
paragraphs.simple: I expect you have seen someone put a lighted match to a bit of newspaper that is propped up against an unlit fire. For a second nothing seems to have happened. Then you notice a tiny streak of flame creeping along the edge of the newspaper. It was like that now. For a second after Aslan had breathed upon him, the stone lion looked just the same. Then a tiny streak of gold began to run along his white marble back. Then it spread. Then the color seemed to lick all over him, as the flame licks all over a bit of paper. Then, while his back legs were still obviously stone, the lion shook his mane, and all the heavy stone folds turned into living hair. Then he opened a great red mouth, warm and living, and gave a huge yawn. And now his back legs had come to life. He lifted one of them and scratched himself. Then, having caught sight of Aslan, he went bounding after him. He jumped round him, whimpering with delight, and jumped up to lick his face.

paragraphs.context: These two Kings and two Queens governed Narnia well
paragraphs.mainIdea: The two Kings and two Queens rule Narnia well for many years. They grow and change, and each is given a title: the Magnificent, the Gentle, the Just and the Valiant.
paragraphs.simple: And now, as you see, this story is nearly (but not quite) at an end. These two Kings and two Queens ruled Narnia well, and long and happy was their reign. At first much of their time was spent in looking for the rest of the White Witch's army and destroying it. For a long time there would be news of evil things hiding in the wilder parts of the forest, a haunting here and a killing there, a glimpse of a werewolf one month and a rumor of a hag the next. But in the end all that foul brood was stamped out. They made good laws and kept the peace. They saved good trees from being cut down for no reason. They freed young dwarfs and young satyrs from being sent to school. They stopped busybodies and interferers, and they helped ordinary people who wanted to live and let live. They drove back the fierce giants on the north of Narnia, quite a different sort from Giant Rumblebuffin, when these came across the border. They made friends and agreements with countries beyond the sea, and paid them visits of state and received visits of state from them. They themselves grew and changed as the years passed over them. Peter became a tall man with a deep chest and a great warrior, and he was called King Peter the Magnificent. Susan grew into a tall and gracious woman with black hair that fell almost to her feet. The kings of the countries beyond the sea began to send ambassadors asking for her hand in marriage. She was called Susan the Gentle. Edmund was a more serious and quieter man than Peter, and great in council and judgment. He was called King Edmund the Just. As for Lucy, she was always gay and golden-haired. All princes in those parts wanted her to be their Queen, and her own people called her Queen Lucy the Valiant.

paragraphs.context: they were no longer Kings and Queens in their hunting array
paragraphs.mainIdea: The four Kings and Queens walk through the trees and come out of the wardrobe. They are children again, on the same day.
paragraphs.simple: So these Kings and Queens entered the thicket. Before they had gone twenty paces, they all remembered that the thing they had seen was called a lamp-post. Before they had gone twenty more, they noticed that they were making their way not through branches but through coats. The next moment they all came tumbling out of a wardrobe door into the empty room. They were no longer Kings and Queens in their hunting clothes, but just Peter, Susan, Edmund and Lucy in their old clothes. It was the same day and the same hour of the day on which they had all gone into the wardrobe to hide. Mrs Macready and the visitors were still talking in the passage. But luckily they never came into the empty room, and so the children were not caught.

paragraphs.context: there lived a poor fisherman called Arsheesh, and with him there lived
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shasta lives with a poor fisherman called Arsheesh. Arsheesh is hard on him when the fish sell badly, and Shasta has a lot of work.
paragraphs.simple: In those days, far south in Calormen, a poor fisherman called Arsheesh lived by a small arm of the sea. A boy lived with him and called him Father. The boy's name was Shasta. On most days Arsheesh went out in his boat in the morning to fish. In the afternoon he put his donkey to a cart and loaded the cart with fish. Then he went about a mile south to the village to sell the fish. If they sold well, he came home in a fairly good mood and said nothing to Shasta. If they sold badly, he found fault with Shasta and maybe hit him. There was always something to find fault with, because Shasta had a lot of work to do. He mended and washed the nets, cooked the supper and cleaned the cottage where they both lived.

paragraphs.context: These were great days for Shasta, and every day better than the last
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shasta gets better at riding, and Bree is a patient teacher. Bree does not like to talk about the Tisroc's wars. He wants to fight in the Narnian wars as a free Horse.
paragraphs.simple: These were very good days for Shasta. Each day was better than the last, because he grew stronger and fell less often. Bree still said Shasta sat like a bag of flour in the saddle. He said he would be ashamed to be seen with Shasta on the main road, even if it was safe. But Bree was a patient teacher, though his words were rude. No one can teach riding as well as a horse. Shasta learned to trot, to canter and to jump. He learned to stay on when Bree stopped or turned to the left or right without warning. Bree said you might have to do that at any moment in a battle. Shasta asked to hear about the battles and wars in which Bree had carried the Tarkaan. Bree told of long forced marches, of crossing fast rivers, and of charges. He told of fierce fights between horsemen, where the war horses fought too. They were all stallions, trained to bite and kick, and to rear up at the right moment. Then the weight of the horse and of the rider came down on the enemy. But Bree did not want to talk about the wars as often as Shasta wanted to hear. He said they were only the Tisroc's wars, and he had fought in them as a slave and a dumb beast. He said he wanted the Narnian wars, where he would fight as a free Horse among his own people.

paragraphs.context: the best place would be the Tombs of the Ancient Kings
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bree says they should meet at the Tombs of the Ancient Kings if they get separated in Tashbaan. Then Hwin says the real problem is how to get through the city.
paragraphs.simple: Bree said the first thing to do was to choose a place on the far side of Tashbaan where they would all promise to meet. They would need it if they were separated while passing the city. He said the best place was the Tombs of the Ancient Kings, on the very edge of the desert. He said they were like great stone beehives and easy to see. He said the best part was that none of the Calormenes would go near them. They think ghouls haunt the place and they are afraid of it. Aravis asked if ghouls did not really haunt it. Bree said he was a free Narnian horse and did not believe these Calormene tales. Then Shasta said he was not a Calormene either, and did not care a straw about these old stories. That was not quite true. It rather impressed Aravis, but at the moment it also annoyed her. She said she did not mind any number of ghouls either. So they agreed that the Tombs would be their meeting place on the other side of Tashbaan. They felt they were getting on well, until Hwin humbly said that the real problem was not where to go after they got through Tashbaan. It was how to get through it.

paragraphs.context: The leader of the fair-haired men suddenly pointed at Shasta
paragraphs.mainIdea: The leader of the fair-haired men calls Shasta their runaway. He seizes him and smacks him.
paragraphs.simple: But there was no time to enjoy the sight, because at once a really dreadful thing happened. The leader of the fair-haired men suddenly pointed at Shasta and cried out that there was their runaway. He seized Shasta by the shoulder. Then he gave Shasta a smack. It was not a cruel one that makes you cry. It was a sharp one that lets you know you are in disgrace. Then he spoke, still shaking Shasta.

paragraphs.context: his first impulse was to say that he was only poor Arsheesh
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shasta cannot say who he is, because people would ask about his horse and Aravis. Bree and Aravis cannot help him.
paragraphs.simple: Shasta's first thought was to say that he was only poor Arsheesh the fisherman's son, and that the foreign lord was wrong. But in that crowded place he did not want to start explaining who he was or what he was doing. People would soon ask where he got his horse and who Aravis was. Then he would lose any chance of getting through Tashbaan. His next thought was to look at Bree for help. But Bree did not want the crowd to know that he could talk, and he looked as stupid as a horse can look. Shasta did not even dare to look at Aravis, for fear of drawing attention. There was no time to think, because the leader of the Narnians spoke at once.

paragraphs.context: He was in fact a Faun, which is a creature Shasta had never seen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shasta sees that the speaker is a Faun, half man and half goat. His name is Tumnus.
paragraphs.simple: A voice spoke to the Kings and Queens. When Shasta turned to look, he nearly jumped out of his skin with surprise. The speaker was one of the queer people he had seen out of the corner of his eye when he came into the room. He was about as tall as Shasta. From the waist up he was like a man. His legs were hairy and shaped like a goat's, and he had a goat's hoofs and a tail. His skin was rather red, and he had curly hair, a short pointed beard and two little horns. He was a Faun, a creature Shasta had never seen a picture of or heard of. His name was Tumnus. Queen Susan's sister Lucy had met him on her very first day in Narnia. He was a good deal older now, because Peter, Susan, Edmund and Lucy had been Kings and Queens of Narnia for several years.
hardWords: out of the corner of his eye

paragraphs.context: It never came into his head to tell these Narnians the whole truth
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shasta does not dare tell the Narnians the truth. He thinks they would never let him leave the house alive, because he has heard their plans.
paragraphs.simple: Shasta never thought of telling the Narnians the whole truth and asking for help. Shasta had been brought up by a hard, closefisted man like Arsheesh. So Shasta was in the habit of never telling grown-ups anything if he could help it. He thought they would always spoil or stop what you were trying to do. He thought the Narnian King might be friendly to the two horses, because they were Talking Beasts of Narnia. But he thought the King would hate Aravis because she was a Calormene. The King would sell her for a slave or send her back to her father. Shasta thought he did not dare to say he was not Prince Corin. He had heard all their plans. If they knew he was not one of them, they would never let him out of the house alive. They would fear that he would tell the Tisroc, and they would kill him. If the real Corin came back, it would all come out. The writer says Shasta had no idea how noble and free-born people behave.

paragraphs.context: A boy in the street made a beastly joke about Queen Susan
paragraphs.mainIdea: Corin tells Shasta what happened to him in the street. He knocked down a boy and the boy's brother, and he got away from the Watch.
paragraphs.simple: Corin says a boy in the street made a bad joke about Queen Susan, so he knocked the boy down. The boy ran howling into a house, and his big brother came out. So Corin knocked the big brother down too. Then they all followed him until they met three old men with spears, called the Watch. He fought the Watch, and they knocked him down. It was getting dark by then. The Watch took him away to lock him up somewhere. He asked them if they would like a stoup of wine, and they said yes. He took them to a wine shop and got them some, and they sat down and drank until they fell asleep. Then he thought it was time to leave, and he came out quietly. He found the first boy, who had started all the trouble, still standing about. So he knocked him down again. After that he climbed a pipe onto the roof of a house and lay quiet until it began to get light. Since then he has been finding his way back. Then he asks if there is anything to drink.
hardWords: I thought it was time for me to be off

paragraphs.context: a huge animal bounded into view. As the moon was behind it
paragraphs.mainIdea: A huge animal jumps between Shasta and the desert and roars toward the desert. The cries of the other creatures stop, and then it turns to Shasta.
paragraphs.simple: Shasta was just going to run when a huge animal jumped into sight between him and the desert. The moon was behind it, so it looked quite black. Shasta did not know what it was. He saw only that it had a very big, shaggy head and four legs. It did not seem to see him. It suddenly stopped, turned its head toward the desert and roared. The roar rang through the Tombs and seemed to shake the sand under Shasta's feet. The cries of the other creatures suddenly stopped, and he thought he heard feet running away. Then the great beast turned to look at Shasta.

paragraphs.context: she never lost her head even for a moment
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aravis does not lose her head when the Narnians take Shasta away. Then a Tarkheena called Lasaraleen passes in a litter, and Aravis makes her first mistake.
paragraphs.simple: This is what had really happened. Aravis saw the Narnians hurry Shasta away, and she was left alone with two horses who very wisely said nothing. She never lost her head, even for a moment. She took Bree's halter and stood still, holding both horses. Her heart was beating as hard as a hammer, but she did nothing to show it. When the Narnian lords had passed, she tried to move on. But before she could take a step, another crier called out, "Way for the Tarkheena Lasaraleen!" Right after him came four armed slaves, and then four men carrying a litter. It had silk curtains that fluttered and silver bells that jingled, and it filled the whole street with the smell of perfume and flowers. After the litter came women slaves in beautiful clothes, and then a few grooms, runners, pages and others like them. And now Aravis made her first mistake.

paragraphs.context: First came the two slaves (deaf and dumb, as Aravis rightly guessed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aravis, hiding behind the sofa, sees who comes in: two slaves with candles, the very fat Tisroc, a tall young man and the new Grand Vizier. The Grand Vizier is the man she is to marry.
paragraphs.simple: First came two slaves, walking backward and carrying the candles. Aravis rightly guessed that they could not hear or speak, so they were used at the most secret meetings. One stood at each end of the sofa. That was good, because now it was harder to see Aravis. A slave was in front of her, and she looked out between his heels. Then came an old man, very fat, in a strange pointed cap. By the cap she knew he was the Tisroc. The smallest jewel he wore was worth more than all the clothes and weapons of the Narnian lords together. But he was so fat, and so covered with frills, pleats, buttons, tassels and charms, that Aravis thought the Narnian clothes (at least for men) looked nicer. After him came a tall young man in a turban with feathers and jewels, with a scimitar in an ivory case at his side. He seemed very excited, and his eyes and teeth flashed fiercely in the candlelight. Last came a little old man with a hump on his back. He had a wrinkled face. She knew with a shudder that he was Ahoshta Tarkaan, the new Grand Vizier and the man she was promised to marry.

paragraphs.context: This very night and in this hour I will take but two hundred horses
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rabadash tells his father his plan. He will ride to Anvard in two days and take it, go on to Cair Paravel, and catch Queen Susan when her ship arrives.
paragraphs.simple: Rabadash says that this very night he will take only two hundred horses and ride across the desert. It will seem to all men that his father knows nothing about it. On the second morning he will be at the gates of King Lune's castle of Anvard in Archenland. They are at peace with Calormen and not ready, and he will take Anvard before they can move. Then he will ride through the pass above Anvard and down through Narnia to Cair Paravel. The High King will not be there. He was getting ready for a raid against the giants on his northern border when Rabadash left. Rabadash will find Cair Paravel, most likely with open gates, and ride in. He will be careful and polite and spill as little Narnian blood as he can. Then he only has to sit there until the Splendor Hyaline comes in with Queen Susan on board. He will catch his lost bird as she steps ashore, swing her into the saddle and ride back to Anvard.

paragraphs.context: I also love none of these things in comparison with the glory and strength of my throne
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Tisroc says he loves the strength of his throne more than anything. If Rabadash wins, they get Archenland. If he fails, the Tisroc has eighteen other sons.
paragraphs.simple: The Tisroc says the Vizier's words are fine and right. He says he also loves none of these things as much as the glory and strength of his throne. If the Prince wins, they will have Archenland, and perhaps Narnia later. If he fails, the Tisroc has eighteen other sons. He says Rabadash, like the eldest sons of kings, was starting to be dangerous. More than five Tisrocs in Tashbaan died before their time, because their eldest sons grew tired of waiting for the throne. He says it is better for Rabadash to cool his blood far away than to boil it at home doing nothing. Then he says he wants to sleep. He tells the Vizier to send the musicians to his room. He also tells him to call back the pardon they wrote for the third cook, because he feels he will have a bad stomach.

paragraphs.context: one of the worst results of being a slave and being forced to do things
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hwin says nothing back to Bree, but she is right. The writer says a slave who is no longer forced almost loses the power to force himself.
paragraphs.simple: Hwin made no answer. Like most mares of good breeding, she was very nervous and gentle, and she was easily put down. But she was quite right. If Bree had had a Tarkaan on his back to make him go on, he would have found he could go for several hours of hard going. The writer says one of the worst results of being a slave is this. When no one forces you any more, you find that you have almost lost the power to force yourself.

paragraphs.context: One of the most terrible noises in the world, a horse's scream
paragraphs.mainIdea: A lion attacks Hwin and Aravis. Shasta has no weapon, but he shouts at the lion, and it suddenly turns and runs away.
paragraphs.simple: Hwin screamed, which is one of the most terrible sounds in the world. Aravis was bent low over Hwin's neck and seemed to be trying to draw her sword. Then Aravis, Hwin and the lion were almost on top of Shasta. Before they reached him, the lion rose on its back legs, larger than you would think a lion could be. It struck at Aravis with its right paw, and Shasta saw all the terrible claws stretched out. Aravis screamed and swayed in the saddle. The lion was tearing her shoulders. Shasta was half mad with horror. He had no weapon, not even a stick or a stone. He managed to stagger toward the lion and shouted at it, as one would at a dog, "Go home! Go home!" For a fraction of a second he was looking right into its wide-open mouth. Then, to his great surprise, the lion stopped itself, turned head over heels, got up and ran away.

paragraphs.context: I was the lion who forced you to join with Aravis
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Voice tells Shasta that it was the lion, and also the cat. It was also the one who pushed his boat to shore when he was a child.
paragraphs.simple: The Voice said it was the lion. Shasta stared with his mouth open and said nothing. The Voice said it was the lion who forced him to join with Aravis. It was the cat who comforted him among the houses of the dead. It was the lion who drove the jackals away while he slept. It was the lion who gave the Horses new strength, from fear, for the last mile, so that he would reach King Lune in time. And it was the lion he does not remember. That lion pushed the boat in which he lay as a child near death. The boat came to shore where a man sat awake at midnight to receive him.

paragraphs.context: Luckily Shasta had lived all his life too far south in Calormen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shasta has not heard the true stories about Aslan. After one look at the Lion's face, he falls at its feet and says nothing.
paragraphs.simple: Shasta had lived all his life too far south in Calormen to have heard the tales whispered in Tashbaan. They were about a dreadful Narnian demon in the form of a lion. He knew none of the true stories about Aslan, the great Lion. Aslan is the son of the Emperor over-the-Sea and the King above all High Kings in Narnia. But after one look at the Lion's face, Shasta slipped out of the saddle and fell at its feet. He could not say anything, but he did not want to say anything, and he knew he did not need to.

paragraphs.context: It was all new and wonderful to Shasta for Calormene food is quite different
paragraphs.mainIdea: Everything in the Dwarfs' house is new to Shasta. After the meal the Dwarfs and Shasta sit outside in the sun.
paragraphs.simple: All this was new and wonderful to Shasta, because Calormene food is quite different. He did not know what the slices of brown stuff were, because he had never seen toast. He did not know the yellow soft thing was butter, because in Calormen you nearly always get oil. The house was also quite different from Arsheesh's dark hut that smelled of fish. It was different from the halls of the palaces in Tashbaan, which had pillars and carpets. The roof was very low, and everything was made of wood. There was a cuckoo-clock, a red-and-white checked tablecloth and a bowl of wild flowers. There were little curtains on the thick-paned windows. It was rather hard to use dwarf cups, plates, knives and forks. So the helpings were very small, but there were many, and Shasta's plate or cup was filled every moment. The Dwarfs kept asking for butter, more coffee, a few more mushrooms or another egg. When they had all eaten as much as they could, the three Dwarfs drew lots for who would do the washing-up, and Rogin was the unlucky one. Then Duffle and Bricklethumb took Shasta outside to a bench along the cottage wall. They stretched out their legs and gave a great sigh of contentment, and the two Dwarfs lit their pipes. The dew was off the grass and the sun was warm. It would have been too hot if there had not been a light breeze.

paragraphs.context: in a second he and the Dwarf were at it hammer and tongs
paragraphs.mainIdea: Corin and the Dwarf Thornbut begin to fight. It stops when Thornbut falls and sprains his ankle, which keeps him from walking or riding for at least a fortnight.
paragraphs.simple: That was enough for a boy like Corin, and in a second he and the Dwarf were fighting hard. It would have been an even match. Corin had longer arms and more height, but the Dwarf was older and tougher. But the fight was never finished, which is the worst of fights on a rough hillside. By very bad luck Thornbut stepped on a loose stone and fell flat on his nose. When he tried to get up, he found he had sprained his ankle. It was a very painful sprain, and it would keep him from walking or riding for at least a fortnight.

paragraphs.context: The unfortunate Rabadash appeared to be suspended from the castle walls
paragraphs.mainIdea: After the battle, everyone laughs at Rabadash, who hangs from a hook on the castle wall. A tear in the back of his chain mail caught on the hook when he jumped down.
paragraphs.simple: Shasta got up, feeling very stiff, and ran toward the sound to see what the joke was. He saw a very odd sight. Rabadash seemed to be hanging from the castle walls. His feet, about two feet from the ground, were kicking wildly. His chain-shirt was pulled up, so that it was tight under the arms and came halfway over his face. He looked like a man caught getting into a stiff shirt that is a little too small. People said later that this was what happened. Early in the battle, a Giant tried to stamp on Rabadash with his spiked boot. It did not crush him, as the Giant meant, but one of the spikes tore the chain mail. So when Rabadash met Edmund at the gate, he had a hole in the back of his hauberk. Edmund pressed him back toward the wall. Rabadash jumped up on a mounting block and hit down at Edmund from above. But there he was an easy mark for every arrow from the Narnian bows, so he decided to jump down. He wanted to look and sound very grand and dreadful as he jumped, crying, "The bolt of Tash falls from above." But he had to jump sideways, because the crowd left no room in front. Then the tear in his hauberk caught on a hook in the wall. Long ago the hook had had a ring for tying horses. So he hung there, like washing hung up to dry, with everyone laughing at him.

paragraphs.context: while Bree spoke they saw an enormous lion leap up from outside
paragraphs.mainIdea: While Bree talks, a huge lion jumps onto the wall and comes quietly toward him from behind. Hwin and Aravis see it and cannot make a sound.
paragraphs.simple: Bree stood with his back to the green wall while he spoke, and the other two faced him. He spoke in a rather superior tone with his eyes half shut. So he did not see the changed look on the faces of Hwin and Aravis. They had good reason to stare with open mouths. While Bree spoke, they saw an enormous lion leap up from outside and stand on top of the green wall. It was a brighter yellow, and bigger, and more beautiful and more alarming than any Lion they had seen. At once it jumped down inside the wall and began to come toward Bree from behind. It made no noise at all. Hwin and Aravis could not make any noise either, as if they were frozen.

paragraphs.context: The scratches on your back, tear for tear, throb for throb
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan tells Aravis why he scratched her. Her scratches were equal to the stripes laid on the back of her stepmother's slave. She needed to know what it felt like.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan says the scratches on Aravis's back were equal to the stripes laid on the back of her stepmother's slave. It was tear for tear, throb for throb and blood for blood. The slave was beaten because of the drugged sleep that Aravis put on her. Aslan says Aravis needed to know what it felt like.

paragraphs.context: A day will come when that boy will save Archenland from the deadliest danger
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cor tells how the Centaur said he would save Archenland. Lord Bar took Cor to sea, and King Lune went after him.
paragraphs.simple: Cor says that when the Centaur saw Corin and him, the Centaur looked at him. The Centaur said that a day would come when that boy would save Archenland from the deadliest danger it ever lay in. His father and mother were very pleased, but someone there was not. This was Lord Bar, who had been Lune's Lord Chancellor. Bar had done something wrong, and the King had had to dismiss him. Nothing else was done to him, and he could go on living in Archenland. But he had been in the pay of the Tisroc and had sent a lot of secret information to Tashbaan. When he heard that Cor would save Archenland from a great danger, he decided Cor must be put out of the way. He kidnapped Cor and rode down the Winding Arrow to the coast. A ship with his own followers was ready for him. He put out to sea with Cor on board. King Lune got wind of it, though not quite in time, and went after him as fast as he could. Lord Bar was already at sea when the King reached the coast, but not out of sight. Within twenty minutes the King was on board one of his own warships.

paragraphs.context: They couldn't help it. Rabadash had been wagging his ears all the time
paragraphs.mainIdea: At Aslan's words, Rabadash's ears, face and arms change until he is a donkey, and everyone laughs. His speech lasts a moment longer than his shape.
paragraphs.simple: They could not help laughing. Rabadash had been wagging his ears all the time, and as soon as Aslan said, "The hour has struck!" the ears began to change. They grew longer and more pointed, and soon had gray hair on them. Everyone was wondering where they had seen ears like that, when Rabadash's face began to change too. It grew longer, and thicker at the top, and the eyes grew larger. The nose sank back into the face, or else the face swelled out and became all nose, and there was hair all over it. His arms grew longer and came down in front of him until his hands rested on the ground. They were not hands now, they were hoofs. He was standing on all fours, and his clothes disappeared. Everyone laughed louder and louder, because now what had been Rabadash was a donkey. The terrible thing was that his human speech lasted just a moment longer than his human shape. So when he saw the change coming over him, he screamed.

paragraphs.context: And in the temple of Tash you shall be healed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan says Rabadash will be healed in the temple of Tash at the Autumn Feast. If he ever goes more than ten miles from the great temple in Tashbaan, he will become a donkey again for good.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan tells Rabadash that he has appealed to Tash, so in the temple of Tash he will be healed. He must stand before the altar of Tash in Tashbaan at the great Autumn Feast this year. There, in the sight of all Tashbaan, his ass's shape will fall from him, and all men will know him for Prince Rabadash. But as long as he lives, if he ever goes more than ten miles away from the great temple in Tashbaan, he will at once be as he is now. And from that second change there will be no return.

paragraphs.context: For this is what it means to be a king: to be first in every desperate attack
paragraphs.mainIdea: King Lune tells Cor what it means to be a king. A king is first in attack and last in retreat. When there is hunger, he wears finer clothes and laughs louder over a smaller meal.
paragraphs.simple: King Lune says that this is truer than Cor's brother knows. He says being a king means to be first in every desperate attack and last in every desperate retreat. It also means that when there is hunger in the land, which must be now and then in bad years, the king wears finer clothes. He also laughs louder over a smaller meal than any man in the land.
