paragraphs.context: Peter, Susan, Edmund, and Lucy, and it has been told in another book
paragraphs.mainIdea: Four children once went through a wardrobe to Narnia and became kings and queens there. When they came back to England, it all seemed to have taken no time.
paragraphs.simple: Once there were four children. Their names were Peter, Susan, Edmund and Lucy. Another book, called The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, tells how they had an unusual adventure. They opened the door of a magic wardrobe and found themselves in a world quite different from ours. In that world they became kings and queens in a country called Narnia. While they were in Narnia, it seemed that they ruled for many years. But when they came back through the door and were in England again, it all seemed to have taken no time at all. In any case, nobody noticed that they had ever been away. They never told anyone, except one very wise grown-up.

paragraphs.context: Pressing their way between the laden branches they reached the wall
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children push through branches to an old wall and a great arch. They go through it into a wide, quiet place with walls all round.
paragraphs.simple: They pushed their way between the loaded branches and came to the wall. It was very old and broken down in some places. Moss and wallflowers grew on it. It was higher than all but the tallest trees. Close to it, they found a great arch. There must once have been a gate in it, but now the largest of all the apple trees almost filled it. They had to break some of the branches to get past. When they had done this, they all blinked, because the daylight was suddenly much brighter. They were in a wide, open place with walls all round it. Here there were no trees, only level grass, daisies, ivy and gray walls. It was a bright, secret, quiet place, and rather sad. All four of them stepped out into the middle of it. They were glad to straighten their backs and move their arms and legs freely.

paragraphs.context: it was the very day before the ambassadors came from the King of Calormen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter gives his fourth point. He asks them to remember planting the orchard at Cair Paravel, and old Lilygloves the mole.
paragraphs.simple: Peter says, “Fourth point.” He asks if they do not remember. It was the very day before the men sent by the King of Calormen came. They planted the orchard outside the north gate of Cair Paravel. Pomona herself, the greatest of all the wood-people, came to put good spells on it. The moles, those very good little fellows, did the actual digging. Can they have forgotten funny old Lilygloves, the chief mole, leaning on his spade and saying, “Believe me, your Majesty, you will be glad of these fruit trees one day”? And Peter says, by Jove, he was right.

paragraphs.context: the ancient treasure chamber of Cair Paravel where they had once reigned
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children find the old treasure room of Cair Paravel. It is cold and covered in dust, and it feels sad. For a minute nobody speaks.
paragraphs.simple: Now they all knew that this was the old treasure room of Cair Paravel, where they had once ruled as Kings and Queens of Narnia. A kind of path ran up the middle, like a path in a greenhouse. All along each side, a little way apart, stood rich suits of armor, like knights guarding the treasures. Between the suits of armor, on each side of the path, were shelves covered with precious things. There were necklaces, arm rings and finger rings, gold bowls and dishes, and long tusks of ivory. There were brooches, small crowns and chains of gold. There were heaps of jewels not yet set in anything, lying in piles anyhow, as if they were marbles or potatoes: diamonds, rubies, carbuncles, emeralds, topazes and amethysts. Under the shelves stood great oak chests with iron bars to make them strong, and heavy locks. It was bitterly cold, and so still that they could hear themselves breathing. The treasures were so covered with dust that, if they had not known where they were and remembered most of the things, they would hardly have known these were treasures. There was something sad and a little frightening about the place, because it all seemed so forgotten and long ago. That was why nobody said anything for at least a minute.

paragraphs.context: however long we seemed to have lived in Narnia, when we got back
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmund starts to explain what puzzled them last night. It was only a year since they left Narnia, but Cair Paravel looks hundreds of years old.
paragraphs.simple: Edmund says, “Why, the whole thing.” He reminds them of what they were puzzling about last night. It was only a year ago since they left Narnia, but everything looks as if nobody had lived in Cair Paravel for hundreds of years. He asks if they do not see it now. They seemed to live in Narnia for a long time, yet when they got back through the wardrobe, it seemed to have taken no time at all.

paragraphs.context: woods along the shore were as full of ghosts as they were of trees
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Dwarf explains that people say the woods are full of ghosts. He never believed it, but the two men who were taking him there did.
paragraphs.simple: The Dwarf says that all his life he has been told that these woods along the shore are as full of ghosts as of trees. That is what the story says. It is also why, when people want to get rid of someone, they usually bring him down here, as they were doing with him, and say they will leave him to the ghosts. But he always wondered if they did not really drown them or cut their throats. He never quite believed in the ghosts. But the two cowards the children had just shot did believe in them. They were more afraid of taking him to his death than he was of going.

paragraphs.context: never let me catch you talking—or thinking either—about all those silly stories
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miraz is angry that Caspian talks about Aslan and the old Kings and Queens. He says none of it was ever true and Caspian must never talk or think of it again.
paragraphs.simple: Miraz tells Caspian to stop that noise. He takes Caspian by the shoulders and gives him a shake. He says, “Stop it.” He says Caspian must never let him catch him talking, or thinking either, about all those silly stories again. He says there never were those Kings and Queens. He asks how there could be two Kings at the same time. He says there is no such person as Aslan, and there are no such things as lions. He says there never was a time when animals could talk. Then he asks, “Do you hear?”

paragraphs.context: All you have heard about Old Narnia is true
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Doctor tells Caspian that the old stories are true. The Telmarines silenced the animals and trees, killed or drove away the Dwarfs and Fauns, and want everyone to forget them.
paragraphs.simple: The Doctor says, “Listen.” All that Caspian has heard about Old Narnia is true. It is not the land of Men. It is the country of Aslan, of the Waking Trees and the Visible Naiads, of Fauns and Satyrs, of Dwarfs and Giants, of the gods and the Centaurs, and of Talking Beasts. The first Caspian fought against these. It is the Telmarines who made the beasts, the trees and the fountains silent. They killed the Dwarfs and Fauns or drove them away. Now they are trying to hide even the memory of them. The King does not allow them to be spoken of.

paragraphs.context: Kings are in deadly fear of the sea because they can never quite forget
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Doctor says the ghost stories about the woods are lies made up by the Telmarines. Their Kings fear the sea, because in the stories Aslan comes from over the sea.
paragraphs.simple: The Doctor says Caspian speaks as he has been taught, but it is all lies. There are no ghosts there. The Telmarines made up that story. Their Kings are in great fear of the sea, because they can never quite forget that in all the stories Aslan comes from over the sea. They do not want to go near it, and they do not want anyone else to go near it. So they have let great woods grow up, to keep their people away from the coast. But they have quarreled with the trees, so they are afraid of the woods. And because they are afraid of the woods, they imagine the woods are full of ghosts. The Kings and great men hate both the sea and the wood. They partly believe these stories, and partly help them along. They feel safer if no one in Narnia dares to go down to the coast and look out to sea, toward Aslan’s land, the morning and the eastern end of the world.

paragraphs.context: Everyone except your Majesty knows that Miraz is a usurper
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Doctor says Miraz is a usurper and not the true King. One by one, Miraz got rid of every lord who could speak for Caspian. Then his flatterers begged him to be King.
paragraphs.simple: The Doctor says he is surprised that Caspian has never asked him why, as the son of King Caspian, he is not King Caspian himself. Everyone except Caspian knows that Miraz is a usurper. When Miraz first began to rule, he did not even pretend to be the King. He called himself Lord Protector. Then Caspian’s royal mother died. She was the good Queen and the only Telmarine who was ever kind to the Doctor. Then, one by one, all the great lords who had known Caspian’s father died or disappeared. It was not by accident. Miraz got them out of the way. Belisar and Uvilas were shot with arrows on a hunting party, and people pretended it was by chance. Miraz sent all the great house of the Passarids to fight giants on the northern border until, one by one, they fell. He had Arlian and Erimon and a dozen more put to death for treason, on a false charge. He locked up the two brothers of Beaversdam as madmen. Finally he talked the seven noble lords into sailing away to look for new lands beyond the Eastern Ocean. They were the only Telmarines who did not fear the sea. As he meant, they never came back. When no one was left who could speak a word for Caspian, Miraz’s flatterers, as he had told them to, begged him to become King. And of course he did.

paragraphs.context: is the greatest and most sacred treasure of Narnia. Many terrors I endured
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Doctor gives Caspian Queen Susan’s magic horn. It may bring strange help, perhaps even Aslan, but Caspian must use it only at his greatest need.
paragraphs.simple: The Doctor says this is the greatest and most holy treasure of Narnia. When he was still young, he went through many terrors and said many spells to find it. It is the magic horn of Queen Susan herself, which she left behind when she vanished from Narnia at the end of the Golden Age. It is said that anyone who blows it will have strange help, and no one can say how strange. It may have the power to call Queen Lucy, King Edmund, Queen Susan and High King Peter back from the past, and they will put everything right. It may be that it will call up Aslan himself. Caspian must take it, but he must not use it except at his greatest need. Then the Doctor says, “And now, haste, haste, haste.” The little door at the very bottom of the Tower, the door into the garden, is unlocked. There they must part.

paragraphs.context: We don’t change. We hold on. I say great good will come of it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Trufflehunter says Dwarfs forget and change, but the beasts do not. He says Caspian is the true King of Narnia.
paragraphs.simple: Trufflehunter tells Nikabrik not to go talking about things he does not understand. He says Dwarfs are as forgetful and changeable as the Humans themselves. He himself is a beast, and a Badger too. He says, “We don’t change. We hold on.” He says great good will come of it. They have the true King of Narnia here: a true King, coming back to true Narnia. And the beasts remember, even if Dwarfs forget, that Narnia was never right except when a Son of Adam was King.

paragraphs.context: Tarva and Alambil have met in the halls of high heaven
paragraphs.mainIdea: Glenstorm says the time has come for war. Tarva and Alambil have met, and a son of Adam has come to rule. Everyone now feels they must fight.
paragraphs.simple: Glenstorm says, “The time is ripe.” He watches the skies, because that is his job, just as remembering is the Badger’s job. Tarva and Alambil have met in the halls of high heaven. On earth a son of Adam has again risen to rule and name the creatures. The hour has come. Their council at Dancing Lawn must be a council of war. He spoke in such a voice that neither Caspian nor the others hesitated for a moment. Now it seemed to them quite possible that they might win a war, and quite certain that they must fight one.

paragraphs.context: lies within the skirts of the Great Woods and it is a huge mound
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doctor Cornelius tells where to go: Aslan’s How, a huge mound at the edge of the Great Woods, with caves inside. It would keep them safe from everything except hunger.
paragraphs.simple: The Doctor says Aslan’s How lies inside the edge of the Great Woods. It is a huge mound that Narnians raised in very ancient times over a very magical place. A very magical Stone stood there, and perhaps still stands. The Mound is hollowed out inside into long passages and caves, and the Stone is in the middle cave. There is room in the Mound for all their stores. The ones who most need cover, and are most used to living underground, can be put in the caves. The rest can lie in the wood. If they must, all of them, except this worthy Giant, could go back into the Mound. There they would be out of the reach of every danger except famine.

paragraphs.context: At last there came a night when everything had gone as badly as possible
paragraphs.mainIdea: Caspian’s biggest battle failed. Wimbleweather the Giant came out at the wrong time and from the wrong place, and many were hurt. The company was sad.
paragraphs.simple: At last there came a night when everything had gone as badly as it could. The rain, which had fallen heavily all day, stopped when night came, only to be followed by raw cold. That morning Caspian had arranged his biggest battle yet, and everyone had put their hopes in it. He, with most of the Dwarfs, was to have attacked the King’s right wing at daybreak. Then, when they were fighting hard, Giant Wimbleweather, with the Centaurs and some of the fiercest animals, was to have broken out from another place and tried to cut the King’s right wing off from the rest of the army. But it had all failed. No one had warned Caspian, because no one in these later days of Narnia remembered, that Giants are not at all clever. Poor Wimbleweather, though as brave as a lion, was a true Giant in that way. He had broken out at the wrong time and from the wrong place, and both his party and Caspian’s had suffered badly and done the enemy little harm. The best of the Bears had been hurt, a Centaur was terribly wounded, and few in Caspian’s party had not lost blood. It was a gloomy company that huddled under the dripping trees to eat their small evening meal.

paragraphs.context: The great thing is to slash at your enemy’s legs and feet
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmund beats Trumpkin in a sword fight with a trick. The air of Narnia has brought back his old skill.
paragraphs.simple: Both swords were out in a moment, and the three others jumped off the dais and stood watching. It was well worth watching. It was not like the stupid fighting with broad swords that you see on the stage, and not even like rapier fighting, which you sometimes see done rather better. This was real broad-sword fighting. The great thing is to cut at your enemy’s legs and feet, because that is the part with no armor. When he cuts at yours, you jump with both feet off the ground, so that his blow goes under them. This gave the Dwarf an advantage, because Edmund was much taller and always had to stoop. The writer does not think Edmund would have had a chance if he had fought Trumpkin twenty-four hours earlier. But the air of Narnia had been working on him ever since they arrived on the island. All his old battles came back to him, and his arms and fingers remembered their old skill. He was King Edmund once more. The two fighters circled round and round and gave stroke after stroke. Susan, who never could learn to like this sort of thing, shouted, “Oh, do be careful.” Then, so quickly that nobody could see how it happened unless they knew, as Peter did, Edmund flashed his sword round with a strange twist. The Dwarf’s sword flew out of his grip, and Trumpkin was shaking his empty hand, as you do after a “sting” from a cricket-bat.

paragraphs.context: When we first discovered Narnia a year ago—or a thousand years ago
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmund votes to go up, as Lucy wants. He says Lucy found Narnia first and no one believed her, but she was right.
paragraphs.simple: Edmund says, speaking quickly and turning a little red, “Well, there is just this.” When they first found Narnia a year ago, or a thousand years ago, whichever it is, Lucy was the first to find it, and none of them would believe her. He was the worst of the lot, he knows. Yet she was right after all. Would it not be fair to believe her this time? He votes for going up.

paragraphs.context: If you go back to the others now, and wake them up
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan tells Lucy that anyone can find out what will happen. She must wake the others, tell them she has seen him, and tell them to follow him.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan says anyone can find out what will happen. Lucy is to go back to the others now and wake them up. She is to tell them she has seen him again, and that they must all get up at once and follow him. Then what will happen? There is only one way of finding out.

paragraphs.context: The sound, deep and throbbing at first like an organ
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan roars, and the sound spreads over all Narnia. Men, animals, the river-god and the trees all wake.
paragraphs.simple: The sound was deep and throbbing at first, like an organ beginning on a low note. It rose and grew louder, and then far louder again, until the earth and air shook with it. It rose from that hill and spread across all Narnia. Down in Miraz’s camp, men woke, stared at one another with white faces, and grabbed their weapons. Down below that, in the Great River, now at its coldest hour, the heads and shoulders of the nymphs and the great weedy-bearded head of the river-god rose from the water. Beyond it, in every field and wood, the alert ears of rabbits rose from their holes, the sleepy heads of birds came out from under wings, owls hooted, vixens barked, hedgehogs grunted, and the trees stirred. In towns and villages mothers pressed babies close to their breasts and stared with wild eyes, dogs cried softly, and men jumped up, feeling about for lights. Far away on the northern border, the mountain giants looked out from the dark doors of their castles.

paragraphs.context: I mean the Witch. Sit down again. Don’t all take fright at a name
paragraphs.mainIdea: Nikabrik says the power he means is the White Witch. He says they need a power on their side, and that the stories say she beat Aslan.
paragraphs.simple: Nikabrik says very slowly and clearly, “Yes, I mean the Witch.” He tells them to sit down again, and not to take fright at a name as if they were children. They want power, he says, and a power that will be on their side. As for power, he asks, do the stories not say that the Witch beat Aslan, tied him up, and killed him on that very Stone over there, just beyond the light?

paragraphs.context: I had meant to refuse it. But I’ll accept it.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miraz had meant to refuse Peter’s challenge. His two lords make him angry, so he says he will accept it.
paragraphs.simple: Miraz roars, “So I am to be an old fool with one foot in the grave, as well as a coward.” He says he will tell his Lords what it is. Their advice, which he calls womanish, always runs away from the true point, which is one of policy. It has made them do the very opposite of what they meant. He had meant to refuse the challenge. But he will accept it. He says, “Do you hear, accept it!” He will not be shamed because some witchcraft or treason has frozen both their bloods.

paragraphs.context: But indeed there was no need to egg the usurper on
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miraz hits Peter on the helmet and Peter falls on one knee. Miraz’s sword comes down at him, but the Dwarf-made mail holds.
paragraphs.simple: Edmund says, “Not he. You don’t know him—Oh!” Miraz had got in a blow at last, on Peter’s helmet. Peter staggered, slipped sideways and fell on one knee. The roar of the Telmarines rose like the noise of the sea. They yelled, “Now, Miraz. Now. Quick! Quick! Kill him.” But there was no need to push the usurper on. He was on top of Peter already. Edmund bit his lips until the blood came, as the sword flashed down at Peter. It looked as if it would cut off his head. But, thank heavens, it had slid off his right shoulder. The mail made by Dwarfs was strong and did not break.

paragraphs.context: Great, strong trunks of ivy came curling up all the piers of the bridge
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bacchus and his people go into the water. Ivy grows up the bridge and breaks it, and everyone crosses at the ford.
paragraphs.simple: “That means the bridge, I expect,” thought Lucy. And so it did. Bacchus and his people splashed forward into the shallow water, and a minute later the most curious things began to happen. Great, strong trunks of ivy came curling up all the piers of the bridge, growing as quickly as a fire grows. They wrapped the stones round, splitting, breaking and pulling them apart. The walls of the bridge turned into hedges, bright with hawthorn, for a moment. Then the whole thing collapsed with a rush and a rumble into the swirling water. With much splashing, screaming and laughter, the revelers waded or swam or danced across the ford. The girls cried, “Hurray! It’s the Ford of Beruna again now!” They went up the bank on the far side and into the town.

paragraphs.context: a shipload of pirates were driven by storm on an island
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan tells Caspian how the Telmarines began. Pirates from the world of Adam’s sons fell through an opening between worlds into Telmar, and the people who came after them later took Narnia.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan says Caspian might have known that he could be no true King of Narnia unless, like the kings of old, he was a son of Adam and came from the world of Adam’s sons. And so he is. Many years ago, in that world, in a deep sea called the South Sea, a storm drove a shipload of pirates onto an island. There they did as pirates would. They killed the people who lived there and took their women as wives. They made palm wine, drank and were drunk, lay in the shade of the palm trees, woke up and quarreled, and sometimes killed one another. In one of these fights, six were chased away by the rest. They ran off with their women to the middle of the island and up a mountain, and went, as they thought, into a cave to hide. But it was one of the magical places of that world, one of the openings between that world and this. There were many such openings between worlds in old times, but they have become rarer. This was one of the last, and Aslan does not say it was the last. So the pirates fell, or rose, or stumbled, or dropped right through, and found themselves in this world, in the Land of Telmar, where no people lived then. Why no people lived there is a long story that Aslan will not tell now. In Telmar those who came after them lived and became a fierce and proud people. After many generations there was a famine in Telmar. They attacked Narnia, which was then in some disorder (that also would be a long story), and they won it in war and ruled it. Aslan asks Caspian, “Do you mark all this well?”

paragraphs.context: After that came a moment which is hard to describe
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children change back into school clothes and say goodbye to their friends and Aslan. They go through the Door and find themselves at the English station again.
paragraphs.simple: It was odd, and not very nice, to take off their royal clothes and go back, in their school clothes, which were not very fresh now, into that great crowd. One or two of the nastier Telmarines laughed at them. But the other creatures all cheered and stood up to honor Peter the High King, Queen Susan of the Horn, King Edmund and Queen Lucy. There were loving farewells, and on Lucy’s part tearful ones, with all their old friends: animal kisses, hugs from Bulgy Bears, hands wrung by Trumpkin, and a last tickly, whiskery hug from Trufflehunter. Of course Caspian offered the Horn back to Susan, and of course Susan told him to keep it. And then, wonderfully and terribly, it was farewell to Aslan himself. Peter took his place, with Susan’s hands on his shoulders, Edmund’s on hers, Lucy’s on his, and the first of the Telmarines’ on Lucy’s. So they moved forward to the Door in a long line. After that came a moment that is hard to describe, for the children seemed to see three things at once. One was the mouth of a cave opening onto the glaring green and blue of an island in the Pacific, where all the Telmarines would find themselves the moment they were through the door. The second was a glade in Narnia, with the faces of Dwarfs and animals, the deep eyes of Aslan, and the white patches on the Badger’s cheeks. The third, which quickly swallowed up the other two, was the gray, gravelly ground of a platform at a country station, and a seat with luggage round it, where they were all sitting as if they had never moved from it. It felt a little flat and dull for a moment after all they had been through, but also, unexpectedly, nice in its own way, with the familiar railway smell, the English sky and the summer school term before them.

paragraphs.context: THERE WAS A BOY CALLED EUSTACE CLARENCE Scrubb, and he almost deserved it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Eustace Clarence Scrubb is a boy with modern parents. He calls them Harold and Alberta, and their house has very little furniture.
paragraphs.simple: There was a boy called Eustace Clarence Scrubb. He almost deserved the name. His parents called him Eustace Clarence, and his teachers called him Scrubb. I cannot tell you what his friends called him, because he had none. He did not call his father and mother ‘Father’ and ‘Mother’. He called them Harold and Alberta. They were very up-to-date and advanced people. They ate no meat, did not smoke and did not drink. They also wore a special kind of underclothes. In their house there was very little furniture and very few clothes on the beds. The windows were always open.

paragraphs.context: Last year, when he had been staying with the Pevensies
paragraphs.mainIdea: Eustace likes to tease the Pevensies about Narnia. He thinks they make it all up.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Still playing your old game?’ said Eustace Clarence. He had been listening outside the door, and now he came into the room with a big smile. Last year he had stayed with the Pevensies. Then he had managed to hear them all talk about Narnia, and he loved to tease them about it. He thought, of course, that they were making it all up. He was far too stupid to make up anything himself, so he did not like that.

paragraphs.context: I swore an oath that, if once I established peace in Narnia
paragraphs.mainIdea: On the day he became king, Caspian made a promise. He said he would sail east for a year and a day to find his father’s friends, or to learn how they died.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Well, on the day I became king, Aslan agreed. I made a promise. I said that if I could make peace in Narnia, I would sail east myself for a year and a day. I would find my father’s friends, or I would learn that they were dead. And if I could, I would punish the men who killed them. These were their names: the Lord Revilian, the Lord Bern, the Lord Argoz, the Lord Mavramorn, the Lord Octesian, the Lord Restimar, and—oh, that other one who is so hard to remember.’

paragraphs.context: hardly had they raised their cups to their lips
paragraphs.mainIdea: Caspian and his friends sit down with a new man. Then his men catch all five visitors very fast.
paragraphs.simple: Caspian thanked the man. But neither he nor the others much liked the look of their new friend. All of them sat down. They had hardly raised their cups to their lips when the black-haired man nodded to his men. Then, as quick as lightning, strong arms were round all five of the visitors. They fought for a moment, but the other side had all the advantages. Soon everyone had no weapons and had their hands tied behind their backs. Only Reepicheep was still fighting. A man held him tight, and he moved about and bit the man hard.

paragraphs.context: they plucked Gumpas out of his chair and deposited him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bern and Drinian throw the Governor’s table to one side. They take Gumpas out of his chair, and Caspian sits in it.
paragraphs.simple: Caspian nodded to Bern and then stood to one side. Bern and Drinian took a step forward. Each took one end of the table. They lifted it and threw it to one side of the hall. It rolled over, and letters, papers, ink-pots, pens and sealing-wax flew everywhere. Then they took Gumpas out of his chair. They were not rough, but they held him as firmly as if their hands were steel. They put him down about four feet away, facing the chair. Caspian sat down in the chair at once. He laid his bare sword across his knees.

paragraphs.context: He began, almost for the first time in his life, to feel lonely
paragraphs.mainIdea: Eustace begins to feel lonely and afraid. He thinks the others may have left him behind on purpose.
paragraphs.simple: But Eustace did not enjoy himself, or not for very long. For almost the first time in his life, he began to feel lonely. At first this feeling grew very slowly. Then he began to worry about the time. There was not the slightest sound. Suddenly he thought that he might have been lying there for hours. Perhaps the others had gone! Perhaps they had let him walk away on purpose, just so they could leave him behind! He jumped up in a panic and started to go down.

paragraphs.context: It reached the pool and slid its horrible scaly chin down over the gravel
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dragon reaches the pool, but it dies before it can drink.
paragraphs.simple: The dragon reached the pool. It put its ugly chin, which was covered in scales, down on the small stones to drink. But before it drank, it made a great croaking or clanging cry. After a few twitches it rolled onto its side. It lay quite still with one claw in the air. A little dark blood ran out of its wide-open mouth. The smoke from its nose turned black for a moment and then floated away. No more came.

paragraphs.context: the bracelet which he had shoved up above his elbow had become strangely tight
paragraphs.mainIdea: Eustace wakes with a pain in his arm. The bracelet on his arm has become strangely tight, and his arm must have swollen.
paragraphs.simple: Eustace slept and slept. What woke him was a pain in his arm. The moon was shining into the mouth of the cave. The bed of treasure seemed to have become much more comfortable. In fact he could hardly feel it at all. At first he did not know why his arm hurt. But after a while he thought of the bracelet that he had pushed up above his elbow. It had become strangely tight. His arm must have swollen while he was asleep. It was his left arm.

paragraphs.context: it only means I had another smaller suit on underneath the first one
paragraphs.mainIdea: Eustace tells how he took off a skin. His feet were still scaly, so he thought he had another skin under it. He took that off too and went to wash.
paragraphs.simple: ‘But just as I was going to put my feet into the water, I looked down. I saw that they were all hard and rough and wrinkled and scaly, just as they had been before. Oh, that is all right, said I. It only means I had another smaller suit on under the first one. I will have to get out of it too. So I scratched and tore again, and this underskin peeled off well. I stepped out and left it lying next to the other one. Then I went down to the well for my bathe.’

paragraphs.context: Great was the rejoicing when Edmund and the restored Eustace
paragraphs.mainIdea: Everyone is glad when Eustace comes back as a boy. They hear his story and do not want to go back for the gold.
paragraphs.simple: Everyone was very happy when Edmund and the boy Eustace walked into the breakfast circle round the camp fire. Now, of course, everyone heard the earlier part of his story. People wondered if the other dragon had killed the Lord Octesian several years ago. Or maybe Octesian himself had been the old dragon. The jewels that Eustace had filled his pockets with in the cave were gone. So were the clothes he had been wearing. No one wanted to go back to that valley for more treasure, and Eustace wanted it least of all.

paragraphs.context: Still it stretched and stretched till its head was over the starboard bulwark
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Sea Serpent does not jump at the ship. It puts its head over the ship and down into the water, so the whole ship is under the arch of its body.
paragraphs.simple: But the Sea Serpent did not jump at them. It shot its head forward across the ship, level with the yard of the mast. Now its head was just next to the fighting-top. Still it stretched and stretched, until its head was over the starboard side. Then it began to come down, not onto the crowded deck but into the water. So the whole ship was under an arch made by the Serpent. Almost at once the arch began to get smaller. On the starboard side the Sea Serpent was now almost touching the side of the Dawn Treader.

paragraphs.context: on the bottom lay a life-size figure of a man, made apparently of gold
paragraphs.mainIdea: At the bottom of a clear pool there is a figure that seems to be made of gold. When the sun comes out, Lucy thinks it is the most beautiful statue she has seen.
paragraphs.simple: The bottom of the pool was made of large grayish-blue stones. The water was very clear. On the bottom lay the figure of a man, as big as a real man. It seemed to be made of gold. It lay face down with its arms stretched out above its head. Just as they looked at it, the clouds opened and the sun shone out. The golden shape was lit up from one end to the other. Lucy thought it was the most beautiful statue she had ever seen.

paragraphs.context: It is folly to think of avoiding an invisible enemy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Reepicheep says it is silly to try to keep away from an enemy that no one can see. He wants to meet the enemy face to face.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Your Majesties all,’ said Reepicheep, ‘hear me. It is silly to think we can keep away from an enemy that we cannot see, however much we creep and hide. If these creatures want to bring us to battle, they will do it. And whatever comes of it, I would rather meet them face to face than be caught by the tail.’

paragraphs.context: her fingers tingled when she touched it as if it were full of electricity
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lucy touches the book on the desk, and her fingers tingle. It is shut with two lead clasps, and it opens easily when she undoes them.
paragraphs.simple: She went up to the desk and put her hand on the book. Her fingers tingled when she touched it, as if it were full of electricity. She tried to open it, but at first she could not. This was only because it was shut with two lead clasps. When she had undone them, it opened easily. And what a book it was!

paragraphs.context: I knew when I let the Duffers make themselves invisible
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Magician says he knew that Lucy would come to take the spell off the Duffers. He was not sure of the day, and being invisible makes him sleepy.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Well, of course I knew, when I let the Duffers make themselves invisible, that you would come soon to take the spell off. I was not quite sure of the exact day. And I was not especially watching this morning. You see, they had made me invisible too. Being invisible always makes me so sleepy. Heigh-ho—there, I am yawning again. Are you hungry?’

paragraphs.context: If by use you mean filling our bellies or our purses
paragraphs.mainIdea: Reepicheep says the Dark Island may be of no use, but they came for honor and adventure. To turn back would hurt the honor of them all.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Use?’ said Reepicheep. ‘Use, Captain? If you mean filling our stomachs or our bags of money, I agree that it will be of no use at all. As far as I know, we did not sail to look for useful things. We came to look for honor and adventure. And here is as great an adventure as any I have ever heard of. If we turn back here, it hurts all our honor a great deal.’

paragraphs.context: we have had a lot of queer adventures on this voyage of ours
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmund is not sure that it is safe to eat the food or to trust the girl. Strange things have happened on their voyage, and things are not always what they seem.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Look here,’ he said. ‘I hope I am not a coward, I mean about eating this food. And I am sure I do not want to be rude. But we have had a lot of strange adventures on this voyage of ours, and things are not always what they seem. When I look in your face, I cannot help believing all you say. But that is just what might happen with a witch too. How are we to know you are a friend?’

paragraphs.context: no wonder, for the days when I was a star had ceased long before
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Old Man says that his name is Ramandu. He was once a star, long before the men on the ship knew this world.
paragraphs.simple: ‘I was a long way above the air, my son,’ said the Old Man. ‘I am Ramandu. But I see that you stare at one another. You have not heard this name. And that is no wonder. The days when I was a star ended long before any of you knew this world. And all the groups of stars in the sky have changed.’

paragraphs.context: When she sinks, I shall swim east with my four paws
paragraphs.mainIdea: Reepicheep says he will go east as long as he can. He will use the ship, then his small boat, and then he will swim.
paragraphs.simple: ‘No. Why should Your Majesty expect it?’ said Reepicheep, in a voice that most people heard. ‘My own plans are made. While I can, I sail east in the Dawn Treader. When she fails me, I paddle east in my small boat. When she sinks, I will swim east with my four paws. And when I can swim no longer, I will sink with my nose to the sunrise. This is if I have not reached Aslan’s country, or gone over the edge of the world in some great waterfall. Then Peepiceek will be the head of the talking mice in Narnia.’

paragraphs.context: here at last the sky did really come down and join the earth
paragraphs.mainIdea: As they go on, the sky looks like a blue wall that joins the earth. It looks more like glass than anything else.
paragraphs.simple: In a flat place with no trees, the sky always looks as if it comes down to meet the grass in front of you. But as they went on, they got a very strange feeling. Here, at last, the sky really did come down and join the earth. It was a blue wall, very bright, but real and hard. It looked more like glass than anything else. Soon they were quite sure of it. It was very near now.

paragraphs.context: I am opening the door in the sky
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan opens the door in the sky. In one moment, the children are back in their own world.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Child,’ said Aslan, ‘do you really need to know that? Come, I am opening the door in the sky.’ Then, all in one moment, the blue wall tore open, like a curtain being torn. A terrible white light came from beyond the sky. They felt Aslan’s mane and a Lion’s kiss on their foreheads. And then they were in the back bedroom in Aunt Alberta’s home in Cambridge.

paragraphs.context: Nobody asked you to come barging in, did they?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jill is angry because Scrubb starts to tell her what to do. She says rude things to him.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Oh, go away and mind your own business,’ she said. ‘Nobody asked you to come barging in, did they? And you are a nice person to start telling us all what we ought to do, are you not? I suppose you mean we ought to spend all our time being nice to Them, and trying to please Them, and waiting on Them like you do.’

paragraphs.context: Jill was one of those lucky people who have a good head for heights
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jill is not afraid of high places. She is angry when Scrubb pulls her back, but then she sees how white his face is, and she looks down on him.
paragraphs.simple: Jill was one of those lucky people who are not afraid of high places. She did not mind at all standing at the edge of a very steep drop. She was rather angry with Scrubb for pulling her back. ‘Just as if I was a kid,’ she said. She pulled her hand out of his. Then she saw how very white his face had turned. She had no respect for him.

paragraphs.context: Crying is all right in its way while it lasts
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jill stops crying and finds that she needs water very much. She hears a small sound that might be water.
paragraphs.simple: Crying is all right for a time, while it lasts. But you have to stop sooner or later, and then you still have to decide what to do. When Jill stopped, she was very, very thirsty. She had been lying on her face, and now she sat up. The birds had stopped singing, and it was very quiet. But there was one small sound that did not stop. It seemed to come from a good way off. She listened with care, and she was almost sure it was the sound of running water.

paragraphs.context: She had been setting her teeth and clenching her fists for a terrible blast
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Lion’s voice gets softer and Jill goes through the air toward Narnia. His breath is so gentle that she does not know when she leaves the ground.
paragraphs.simple: The voice had been getting softer toward the end of this speech, and now it was gone. Jill looked behind her. She saw that the cliff was already more than a hundred yards behind her, and the Lion himself was a tiny spot of bright gold on the edge of it. She had been holding her teeth together and making her hands into fists, ready for a terrible blast of the Lion’s breath. But the breath had been so gentle that she had not even noticed when she left the ground. And now there was nothing but air for thousands and thousands of feet below her.

paragraphs.context: a little chair on wheels, and, harnessed to it, a little donkey
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jill sees an old, fat Dwarf in a little chair pulled by a little donkey. He is dressed as richly as the King, and his big head is bald.
paragraphs.simple: Right in front of the King there was a little chair with wheels. A little donkey was tied to it, and it was not much bigger than a big retriever dog. The King had turned round to speak to his people before going on board the ship. In the chair sat a fat little Dwarf. He was dressed as richly as the King. But he was fat and sat in a bunch among the cushions, so he looked quite different. He looked like a small shapeless bundle of fur and silk and velvet. He was as old as the King, but stronger and healthier, with very sharp eyes. His head had no hair and was very big. In the light of the sunset it shone like a huge billiard ball.

paragraphs.context: You must get away from here at once. I’ll go and wake
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Owl says there is no time to waste. Jill must leave at once. He will wake the other human, and Jill must change into clothes she can travel in.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Good!’ said the Owl. ‘Then there is no time to lose. You must get away from here at once. I will go and wake the other human. Then I will come back for you. You had better change those court clothes and put on something you can travel in. I will be back very soon. Tu-whoo!’ And without waiting for an answer, he was gone.

paragraphs.context: She had been a great lady, wise and gracious and happy
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Queen has died, and all Narnia is sad. Prince Rilian rides in the north to hunt for the poison worm that killed her, and after a month people see a change in him.
paragraphs.simple: They took the dead Queen back to Cair Paravel. Rilian and the King and all Narnia were very sad. She had been a great lady, wise and kind and happy. She was King Caspian’s bride, whom he had brought home from the east end of the world. People said that she had star blood in her. The Prince took his mother’s death very hard, as well he might. After that he was always riding in the north of Narnia, looking for the poison worm that killed her, to kill it. No one said much about this. The Prince came home from these trips looking tired and upset. But about a month after the Queen’s death, some people said they could see a change in him. There was a look in his eyes like a man who has seen visions. He was out all day, but his horse did not look as if it had been ridden hard. His chief friend among the older men at court was Lord Drinian, who had been his father’s captain on the great trip to the east.

paragraphs.context: Jill had to pinch herself to keep awake, for she knew that if
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jill is so tired that she nearly sleeps on the Owl’s back. At last she gets down and calls Puddleglum.
paragraphs.simple: Jill had to pinch herself to stay awake. She knew that if she slept on Glimfeather’s back, she would probably fall off. At last the two owls stopped flying. She climbed down from Glimfeather, stiff from the ride, and found herself on flat ground. A cold wind was blowing, and there seemed to be no trees. ‘Tu-whoo, tu-whoo!’ called Glimfeather. ‘Wake up, Puddleglum. Wake up. It is the Lion’s business.’

paragraphs.context: Those eels will take a mortal long time to cook
paragraphs.mainIdea: Puddleglum says the eels will take a long time to cook. He will not tell a sad story, so he talks about plans to keep their minds off food.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Now,’ said Puddleglum. ‘Those eels will take a very long time to cook, and one of you might faint from hunger before they are ready. I knew a little girl once. But I had better not tell you that story. It might make you sad, and I never do that. So, to take your minds off your hunger, we may as well talk about our plans.’

paragraphs.context: That night they bivouacked on the bare moor
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children and Puddleglum sleep on the cold hard ground. Puddleglum says it will be colder later, which does not help.
paragraphs.simple: That night they slept in the open on the bare moor. Puddleglum showed the children how to make the best use of their blankets by sleeping back to back. Your backs keep each other warm, and then you can have both blankets on top. But it was still cold, and the ground was hard and not flat. The Marsh-wiggle told them they would feel better if they thought how much colder it would be later and farther north. But this did not cheer them up at all.

paragraphs.context: THERE IS NO DENYING IT WAS A BEAST OF A DAY
paragraphs.mainIdea: The weather is terrible. It is cold, there is snow in the clouds, and the road is broken.
paragraphs.simple: No one can say it was not a terrible day. Above them was a sky with no sun, covered with clouds heavy with snow. On the ground was a black frost. And a wind blew over it that felt as if it would take your skin off. When they came down into the plain, they found that this part of the old road was in much worse shape than any they had seen. They had to find their way over large broken stones, and between big rocks, and across small broken stones. It was hard going for sore feet. And, however tired they got, it was much too cold to stop.

paragraphs.context: I hope you won’t lose all interest in Jill for the rest
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jill cries because she is cold and tired. Crying helps her at that moment.
paragraphs.simple: I hope you will not stop caring about Jill for the rest of the book if I tell you that at this time she began to cry. She had good reasons. Her feet and hands and ears and nose were only just starting to get warm again. Melted snow was running off her clothes. She had had almost nothing to eat or drink that day. Her legs hurt so much that she felt she could not stand much longer. Anyway, it did her more good than anything else would have done, because the Queen said:

paragraphs.context: At lunchtime something happened which made all three of them more anxious
paragraphs.mainIdea: At lunch something happens that makes all three travelers want even more to leave the castle of the Gentle Giants.
paragraphs.simple: At lunch, something happened. It made all three of them want even more to leave the castle of the Gentle Giants. They had lunch in the great hall at a little table of their own, near the fire. At a bigger table, about twenty yards away, six old giants were having lunch. They were so noisy, and their voices were so high in the air, that the children soon paid no more attention to them than you would to car horns outside the window or street noises. They were eating cold deer meat. Jill had never tasted it before, and she liked it.

paragraphs.context: It was pitch black in there, except for the gray light in the opening
paragraphs.mainIdea: The three hide in a cave and fill the opening with stones. The dogs come, and the cave is soon dark.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Quick, quick. Stones. Fill the opening,’ said Puddleglum’s voice in the dark beside her. It was very dark in there, except for the gray light in the opening where they had crawled in. The other two were working hard. She could see Scrubb’s small hands and the Marsh-wiggle’s big hands, black against the light. They were working fast to put stones in a pile. Then she understood how important this was. She looked for large stones herself and gave them to the others. Before the dogs were at the mouth of the cave, they had it nearly full. And now there was no light at all.

paragraphs.context: At last their ship was brought alongside a quay and made fast
paragraphs.mainIdea: The three travelers are taken to a sad city of Earthmen. The Earthmen are busy and no one is interested in them.
paragraphs.simple: At last their ship came to a stop beside a quay (a place for ships) and was tied there. The three travelers were taken to land and marched up into the City. Crowds of Earthmen, no two the same, pushed against them in the busy streets. The sad light fell on many sad and strange faces. But no one showed any interest in the strangers. Every gnome seemed to be as busy as it was sad. Jill never found out what they were so busy about. But the endless moving, pushing and hurrying and the soft pad-pad-pad went on.

paragraphs.context: the heavy, tangled, cold, clammy web of evil magic
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Knight speaks about the magic that holds him. He remembers a pool above ground with trees and sky in it.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Ah,’ he groaned. ‘Spells, spells. A heavy, tangled, cold, wet net of evil magic. Buried alive. Pulled down under the earth, down into the black dark. How many years is it? Have I lived ten years, or a thousand years, in the pit? Maggotmen all around me. Oh, have mercy. Let me out, let me go back. Let me feel the wind and see the sky. There used to be a little pool. When you looked down into it, you could see all the trees growing upside down in the water, all green, and under them, very deep, the blue sky.’

paragraphs.context: the sweet, heavy smell grew very much less
paragraphs.mainIdea: Part of the fire is put out. The sweet smell gets weaker, and the smell of burnt Marsh-wiggle makes everyone think more clearly.
paragraphs.simple: First, the sweet, heavy smell became much less. The whole fire had not been put out, but a good part of it had. What was left smelled mostly of burnt Marsh-wiggle. That is not a nice smell at all. At once everyone’s head was much clearer. The Prince and the children held up their heads again and opened their eyes.

paragraphs.context: it had begun and increased so gradually that they did not know when
paragraphs.mainIdea: A noise grew so slowly that nobody knew when it started. It became a loud roar.
paragraphs.simple: They had all been hearing the noise, but it had started and grown so slowly that they did not know when they first noticed it. For a time it was only a faint, uneasy sound like gentle winds, or like traffic very far away. Then it grew to a low sound like the sea. Then came deep rolling sounds and rushing sounds. Now there seemed to be voices too, and also a steady roar that was not voices.

paragraphs.context: It would have been nasty enough at the bottom even five minutes later
paragraphs.mainIdea: The riders gallop down into a valley where water is rising. They get across just in time.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Hurry,’ cried the Prince. They rode fast down the slope. It would have been bad enough at the bottom even five minutes later. The tide was running up the valley like a fast stream, and if it had come to swimming, the horses could hardly have got across. But the water was still only a foot or two deep. It splashed terribly round the horses’ legs, but they reached the other side safely.

paragraphs.context: She was already in the middle of a crowd when she said this
paragraphs.mainIdea: Many Narnian animals run to Jill. The last to come is a great Panther.
paragraphs.simple: She was already in the middle of a crowd when she said this. Besides the dancers, all kinds of people who had been watching the dance, and whom she had not seen at first, came running up. Squirrels came out of the trees in great numbers, and so did Owls. Hedgehogs came walking from side to side as fast as their short legs could carry them. Bears and Badgers came more slowly. A great Panther, moving its tail in excitement, was the last to join the party.

paragraphs.context: You cannot want wrong things any more, now that you have died, my son
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan tells Caspian that he can see the world of Jill and Eustace for five minutes. In that time he can put things right.
paragraphs.simple: ‘You cannot want wrong things any more, now that you have died, my son,’ said Aslan. ‘And you will see their world for five minutes of their time. It will take no longer than that for you to put things right there.’ Then Aslan told Caspian what Jill and Eustace were going back to, and all about Experiment House. He seemed to know it as well as they did.

paragraphs.context: what weak chests Apes always have and how easily they catch cold
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shift says he will go into the cold water himself, but he will probably die. He says Apes have weak chests, and Puzzle will be sorry.
paragraphs.simple: ‘You want me to go into the water,’ said the Ape. ‘As if you did not know very well what weak chests Apes always have and how easily they catch cold! Very well. I will go in. I already feel cold enough in this cruel wind. But I will go in. I will probably die. Then you will be sorry.’ And Shift’s voice sounded as if he was just going to burst into tears.

paragraphs.context: It was just on the tip of my tongue, only the sign itself came
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Ape says the thunder and the shaking ground are a sign that points the other way. He tells Puzzle to do it now, and asks what a donkey could know about signs.
paragraphs.simple: ‘No, no,’ said the Ape. His mind worked very quickly. ‘It is a sign the other way. I was just going to say that if the real Aslan, as you call him, wanted us to go on with this, he would send us a clap of thunder and a shaking of the earth. It was just on the tip of my tongue, but the sign came before I could get the words out. You have got to do it now, Puzzle. And please do not let us have any more arguing. You know you do not understand these things. What could a donkey know about signs?’
hardWords: on the tip of my tongue

paragraphs.context: shuddering time after time as if under repeated blows
paragraphs.mainIdea: A Dryad shakes and falls dead when her tree is cut down, miles away. Tirian, the Unicorn and the Centaur see it.
paragraphs.simple: ‘A-a-a-h,’ gasped the Dryad. She shook as if in pain. She shook again and again, as if someone was hitting her. Then all at once she fell to one side, as suddenly as if both her feet had been cut from under her. For a second they saw her lying dead on the grass, and then she vanished. They knew what had happened. Her tree, miles away, had been cut down.

paragraphs.context: They put a rope halter round Jewel’s neck
paragraphs.mainIdea: Calormene men take Tirian’s sword and gold crown and tie his hands. They put a rope halter on Jewel and lead the two prisoners uphill.
paragraphs.simple: Then the dark men came round them in a thick crowd. They smelled of garlic and onions, and their white eyes flashed in a frightening way in their brown faces. They put a rope halter round Jewel’s neck. They took the King’s sword away and tied his hands behind his back. One of the Calormenes had a helmet and not a turban, and he seemed to be in command. He snatched the thin gold crown off Tirian’s head and quickly put it away somewhere in his clothes. They led the two prisoners uphill to a place where there was a big clearing. And this was what the prisoners saw.

paragraphs.context: It would have broken your heart with very pity to see their faces
paragraphs.mainIdea: All the Talking Beasts look very sad. Only one does not.
paragraphs.simple: You know how sad your own dog’s face can look sometimes. Think of that, and then think of the faces of all those Talking Beasts, the Birds, Bears, Badgers, Rabbits, Moles and Mice. They were honest, humble and bewildered, and they were all much sadder than that dog. Every tail was down, and every whisker hung low. It would have broken your heart with pity to see their faces. Only one of them did not look at all unhappy.

paragraphs.context: what worried him worst at the moment
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Calormenes tie King Tirian to a tree. What worries him most is a small thing: he cannot wipe the blood from his lip.
paragraphs.simple: The King was so dizzy from being knocked down that he hardly knew what was happening until the Calormenes untied his wrists. They put his arms straight down by his sides and set him with his back against an ash tree. Then they tied ropes round his ankles and knees and waist and chest, and left him there. What worried him most at that time was a small thing, and small things are often the hardest to stand. His lip was bleeding where they had hit him, and he could not wipe the little trickle of blood away, although it tickled him.

paragraphs.context: Without knowing why, he began to feel a faint hope
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tirian feels a little hope. He asks Aslan to send help from beyond the world, and then he calls out.
paragraphs.simple: There was still no change in the night or the wood. But there began to be a kind of change inside Tirian. Without knowing why, he began to feel a faint hope. And he felt somehow stronger. ‘Oh Aslan, Aslan,’ he whispered. ‘If you will not come yourself, at least send me the helpers from beyond the world. Or let me call them. Let my voice go beyond the world.’ Then, hardly knowing that he was doing it, he suddenly cried out in a great voice.

paragraphs.context: They had in fact simply appeared from nowhere
paragraphs.mainIdea: Two children suddenly stand in front of Tirian. They look like the youngest two of the seven people he saw in his dream.
paragraphs.simple: But his sadness did not last long. Almost at once there was a bump, and then a second bump, and two children were standing in front of him. A second before, the wood in front of him had been quite empty. He knew they had not come from behind his tree, because he would have heard them. They had simply come from nowhere. He saw at a glance that they were wearing the same strange, dull clothes as the people in his dream. He saw, at a second look, that they were the youngest boy and girl of that group of seven.

paragraphs.context: Then he sauntered out boldly in full view of the enemy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tirian tells the other two to wait. He walks out boldly in front of a Calormene guard.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Wait here until I come again,’ he whispered to the other two. ‘If I fail, run away.’ Then he walked out in a bold, relaxed way where the enemy could see him. The man jumped when he saw him and was just going to stand up. He was afraid that Tirian might be one of his own officers, and that he would be in trouble for sitting down. But before he could get up, Tirian was down on one knee beside him, saying:

paragraphs.context: Everyone crowded round him and welcomed him and praised him
paragraphs.mainIdea: The group is glad to have one Dwarf with them. But the two children are too tired to stay happy.
paragraphs.simple: Everyone came round him and welcomed him and said good things about him and hit him on the back in a friendly way. One Dwarf could not make a very big difference, of course. But it was very cheering to have even one. The whole group became more cheerful. But Jill and Eustace did not stay cheerful for very long. They were now yawning very much and were too tired to think about anything but bed.

paragraphs.context: Twenty great ships of Calormen put in there in the dark of the night
paragraphs.mainIdea: Farsight tells the King that Cair Paravel is full of dead Narnians and living Calormenes. Twenty Calormene ships took it from the sea, and the people run into the woods.
paragraphs.simple: ‘I have seen two things,’ said Farsight. ‘One was Cair Paravel full of dead Narnians and living Calormenes. The Tisroc’s flag was moving forward along your royal walls, and your people were running from the city, this way and that, into the woods. Cair Paravel was taken from the sea. Twenty great ships of Calormen came in there in the dark of the night before last night.’

paragraphs.context: And they might gradually get stronger and stronger
paragraphs.mainIdea: Some of the group talk about hiding in the woods and growing stronger. Later they could drive the Calormenes out, as happened in the time of King Miraz.
paragraphs.simple: Why not hide in the woods, or even up in the Western Waste beyond the great waterfall, and live like outlaws? They might slowly get stronger and stronger, because Talking Beasts and Archenlanders would come to them every day. At last they would come out of hiding and drive the Calormenes out of the country. The Calormenes would have become careless by then. Narnia would be alive again. After all, something very like that had happened in the time of King Miraz!

paragraphs.context: Don’t blame me if he swallows you whole or blasts you into a cinder
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Ape says anyone can go into the stable, one at a time. He warns that the one inside may swallow them whole or blast them into a cinder.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Anyone can go in,’ he said. ‘But one at a time. Who will go first? He did not say he was feeling very kind. He has been licking his lips a lot since he swallowed up the bad King the other night. He has been growling a lot this morning. I would not much like to go into that stable myself tonight. But just as you like. Who would like to go in first? Do not blame me if he swallows you whole or blasts you into a cinder with the mere terror of his eyes. That is your business. Now then! Who is first? What about one of you Dwarfs?’

paragraphs.context: Then, just as Ginger had done, Emeth came walking forward
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emeth walks forward, as Ginger did, into the open grass between the bonfire and the stable. Jewel says he almost loves this young Calormene warrior, who deserves a better god than Tash.
paragraphs.simple: Then, just as Ginger had done, Emeth came walking forward into the open strip of grass between the bonfire and the stable. His eyes were shining, his face was very serious, his hand was on his sword, and he held his head high. Jill felt like crying when she looked at his face. And Jewel whispered in the King’s ear, ‘By the Lion’s Mane, I almost love this young warrior, though he is a Calormene. He is worthy of a better god than Tash.’

paragraphs.context: It was so lovely that it made you want to cry
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Talking Dogs come to help, and then small animals, the Bear and the Boar come too. Eustace begins to hope, but Tirian sees how few animals have moved.
paragraphs.simple: It was so lovely that it made you want to cry. This, at last, was the sort of thing they had been hoping for. A moment later, several small animals (mice and moles and a squirrel or so) came running up, squealing with joy and saying, ‘See, see. We are here.’ After that the Bear and the Boar came too. Eustace began to feel that perhaps, after all, everything might be going to come right. But Tirian looked round and saw how very few of the animals had moved.

paragraphs.context: the enemy had been edging him to the stable on purpose
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tirian sees that he is fighting at the door of the stable. The enemy has been pushing him there on purpose.
paragraphs.simple: All at once everything was quite clear. He found he was fighting the Tarkaan himself. The bonfire, or what was left of it, was straight in front. He was in fact fighting in the very doorway of the stable. The door had been opened, and two Calormenes were holding it, ready to slam it shut the moment he was inside. He remembered everything now, and he saw that the enemy had been edging him toward the stable on purpose ever since the fight began. And while he was thinking this, he was still fighting the Tarkaan as hard as he could.

paragraphs.context: The door was simply standing up by itself as if it had grown there
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tirian sees a wooden door with a frame, and nothing else around it. It stands in the open air.
paragraphs.simple: Tirian looked and saw the strangest and silliest thing you can think of. Only a few yards away, clear in the sunlight, there stood a rough wooden door, and round it the frame of the door. There was nothing else, no walls and no roof. He walked toward it, not understanding. The others followed him, watching to see what he would do. He walked round to the other side of the door. But it looked just the same from that side. He was still in the open air, on a summer morning. The door was standing up by itself, as if it had grown there like a tree.

paragraphs.context: They are people (Edmund and Lucy had once met one)
paragraphs.mainIdea: In Narnia, stars are shining people. They rush down in a shower and stand behind the group.
paragraphs.simple: The last few seconds before the rain of stars ended were very exciting. Stars began to fall all round them. But in that world stars are not great balls of fire, as they are in ours. They are people. Edmund and Lucy had once met one. So now they found showers of shining people, all with long hair like burning silver and spears like white-hot metal. They rushed down to them out of the black air, faster than falling stones. They made a hissing noise as they landed, and they burned the grass. And all these stars glided past them and stood somewhere behind, a little to the right.

paragraphs.context: It was only a shadow or a copy of the real Narnia which has
paragraphs.mainIdea: Digory says the old Narnia was only a shadow or copy of the real Narnia. All of the old Narnia that mattered has been taken into the real one.
paragraphs.simple: ‘The Eagle is right,’ said the Lord Digory. ‘Listen, Peter. When Aslan said you could never go back to Narnia, he meant the Narnia you were thinking of. But that was not the real Narnia. That had a beginning and an end. It was only a shadow or a copy of the real Narnia, which has always been here and always will be here. Our own world, England and all, is also only a shadow or copy of something in Aslan’s real world. You need not mourn over Narnia, Lucy. All of the old Narnia that mattered, all the dear creatures, have been drawn into the real Narnia through the Door. And of course it is different. It is as different as a real thing is from a shadow, or as waking life is from a dream.’ His voice stirred everyone like a trumpet as he spoke these words. But then he added, under his breath, ‘It’s all in Plato, all in Plato: bless me, what do they teach them at these schools!’ And the older ones laughed. It was so like the things they had heard him say long ago in that other world, where his beard was gray and not golden. He knew why they were laughing and joined in the laugh himself. But very quickly they all became serious again. As you know, there is a kind of happiness and wonder that makes you serious. It is too good to waste on jokes.

paragraphs.context: This was his father, young and merry, as he could just remember him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tirian sees his father, the good King Erlian, as he was when Tirian was a small boy.
paragraphs.simple: It was his own father, the good King Erlian. But he was not as Tirian had seen him last, when they brought him home pale and wounded from his fight with the giant. He was not as Tirian remembered him in his later years either, when he was a gray-headed warrior. This was his father, young and merry, as Tirian could just remember him from very early days. Then he himself had been a little boy playing games with his father in the castle garden at Cair Paravel, just before bedtime on summer evenings. The very smell of the bread and milk he used to have for supper came back to him.

paragraphs.context: You never saw a donkey look feebler and sillier than Puzzle did
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan calls Puzzle the Donkey first. Puzzle looks small and silly next to Aslan. Aslan whispers to him, and Puzzle’s ears go down and then up.
paragraphs.simple: And the very first person that Aslan called to him was Puzzle the Donkey. You never saw a donkey look weaker and sillier than Puzzle did as he walked up to Aslan. Next to Aslan, he looked as small as a kitten next to a St. Bernard. The Lion bowed down his head and whispered something to Puzzle. At that, Puzzle’s long ears went down. But then Aslan said something else, and at that the ears went up again. The humans could not hear what he had said either time. Then Aslan turned to them and said:

paragraphs.context: Strike the bell and bide the danger
paragraphs.mainIdea: This line is part of a short poem cut in the stone. It tells a stranger to hit the bell and wait for the danger.
paragraphs.simple: Hit the bell and wait for the danger.

paragraphs.context: Wrong will be right, when Aslan comes in sight
paragraphs.mainIdea: This line starts an old poem. It says that wrong things will turn right when Aslan can be seen.
paragraphs.simple: Bad things will become right when Aslan comes where people can see him.

paragraphs.context: We got into the letter E in me
paragraphs.mainIdea: The trenches they walked in were the lines of a huge letter E in the words UNDER ME, written across the ruined city.
paragraphs.simple: Scrubb says they did see the writing. They walked inside the letter E of the word me. The low lane was the bottom line of the E, going north. They turned right along the tall line, then right again along the middle line, and came back. He says they were fools. Jill had hoped the words were put there only after they had passed, so the fault would not be theirs. He says that is not so. They had four signs, and they missed the first three.

paragraphs.context: Though under Earth and throneless now I be
paragraphs.mainIdea: This old poem uses under me in two ways. The king is buried under the earth, and while he lived the earth was under his rule.
paragraphs.simple: Though I am under the earth now and have no throne, while I lived all the earth was under me.

sentences.context: It could hardly have been grubbier if he had first rubbed his hands in the earth
sentences.simple: His face could hardly have been dirtier if he had first rubbed his hands in the earth, then had a good cry, and then dried his face with his hands.
sentences.grammar: 'Could hardly have been dirtier' means it was almost as dirty as possible; 'if he had first rubbed ...' imagines what he might have done.

sentences.context: If vacuum cleaners had been invented in those days Polly would have thought
sentences.simple: Vacuum cleaners were not invented then. If they had been, Polly would have thought the sound was a Hoover working a long way off, several rooms away and several floors below.
sentences.grammar: 'If + had been invented, would have thought' talks about something that did not happen: they were not invented, so Polly did not think that.

sentences.context: for the door had been made for getting in, not for getting out
sentences.simple: There was no bolt or handle on this side of the door, because it had been made for getting in, not for getting out.
sentences.grammar: 'Had been made' is 'had been + past form' (it was made before that time); 'for + -ing' says what the door was for.

sentences.context: Polly was very surprised because up till now there had never been any children in that house
sentences.simple: Polly was very surprised, because until now there had never been any children in that house. Only Mr. Ketterley and Miss Ketterley lived there.
sentences.grammar: 'Had never been' ('had + past form') means that up to that moment in the past it was never so; 'up till now' means 'until now'.

sentences.context: that had ever happened to Digory even in a nightmare, that he let out a scream
sentences.simple: It was so sudden, and so horribly unlike anything that had ever happened to Digory, even in a nightmare, that he screamed.
sentences.grammar: 'So ... that' shows a result: it was so sudden and strange that he screamed; 'had ever happened' looks back over all his past.

sentences.context: if someone else will go after her, wearing a yellow ring himself
sentences.simple: She can get back if someone else is willing to go after her. He must wear a yellow ring himself and take two green rings, one to bring himself back and one to bring her back.
sentences.grammar: 'If someone else will go' uses 'will' in the if-part to mean 'is willing to go'; 'wearing' and 'taking' tell how he must go.

sentences.context: A man at my time of life, and in my state of health, to risk the shock
sentences.simple: Uncle Andrew asks: Should a man of my age and my state of health risk the shock and the dangers of being thrown suddenly into a different universe?
sentences.grammar: This is a question with no 'should'. It means 'Should a man of my age ... risk ...?'

sentences.context: he was neither dripping nor panting for breath as anyone would expect
sentences.simple: He was not dripping with water and he was not out of breath, as anyone would expect after being under water.
sentences.grammar: 'Neither ... nor' means not this and not that; 'as anyone would expect' says it is what people normally think.

sentences.context: if we can get back to our own world by jumping into this pool, mightn’t we get somewhere else
sentences.simple: If we can get back to our own world by jumping into this pool, maybe we can get somewhere else by jumping into one of the other pools.
sentences.grammar: 'Mightn't we ...?' is a question that means 'maybe we can'; 'by + -ing' tells how (by jumping).

sentences.context: a place that isn’t in any of the worlds, but once you’ve found that place
sentences.simple: This wood might be the same: a place that is not in any of the worlds. But once you have found that place, you can get into all of them.
sentences.grammar: 'Once you’ve found' (once + present perfect) means 'after you have found'; 'but' shows a different idea from the first part.

sentences.context: the chances would have been a hundred to one against their ever finding it again
sentences.simple: If they had left the pool that led to our own world without making some sort of landmark, it would have been a hundred to one against their ever finding it again.
sentences.grammar: 'If they had left ..., it would have been ...' talks about something that did not happen; 'a hundred to one against' means very unlikely.

sentences.context: If only Digory had remembered what he himself had said a few minutes ago
sentences.simple: Digory had said a few minutes earlier that this was an enchanted room. If he had remembered that, he might have guessed that the enchantment was beginning to work.
sentences.grammar: 'If only + had + past form' shows a wish about the past: he did not remember it; 'might have guessed' means it was possible.

sentences.context: We shall always be wondering what else would have happened if we had struck the bell
sentences.simple: We will always be wondering what else would have happened if we had struck the bell.
sentences.grammar: 'Shall always be wondering' means it goes on and on in the future; 'would have happened if we had struck' talks about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: If we are not out of it in a few minutes we shall be buried under the ruin
sentences.simple: If we are not out of the palace in a few minutes, we will be buried under the ruin.
sentences.grammar: 'If + present, shall be + past form' is a real future condition; 'shall be buried' means the ruin will fall on us and bury us.

sentences.context: there was a word which, if spoken with the proper ceremonies, would destroy all living things
sentences.simple: There was a word that would destroy all living things, except the one who spoke it, if it was spoken with the proper ceremonies.
sentences.grammar: 'If spoken' is short for 'if it was spoken'; 'which ... would destroy' tells what the word could do.

sentences.context: though it were a thousand years, till one came and struck the bell and awoke me
sentences.simple: Jadis had put strong spells on the hall. They made her sleep among the images like an image herself, with no need of food or fire, even for a thousand years, until someone came and struck the bell and woke her.
sentences.grammar: 'Though it were' is an old way to say 'even if it was' (an imagined case); 'neither ... nor' means not this and not that; 'till' means 'until'.

sentences.context: any more than you’d be afraid of a worm after you had met a rattlesnake
sentences.simple: After seeing the two together, you would never again be afraid of Uncle Andrew. You would be no more afraid of him than of a worm after meeting a rattlesnake, or of a cow after meeting a mad bull.
sentences.grammar: 'No more ... than' puts two things side by side: you are not afraid of the first, just as you are not afraid of the second; 'after you had met' shows the meeting comes first.

sentences.context: I will lay such spells on you that anything you sit down on will feel like red hot iron
sentences.simple: At the first sign that you do not obey, I will put such spells on you that anything you sit on will feel like red hot iron. Whenever you lie in a bed, there will be invisible blocks of ice at your feet.
sentences.grammar: 'Such ... that' shows a result: the spells will be so strong that these things happen; 'whenever' means every time.

sentences.context: It must have been a terrible moment for the Witch when she suddenly realized
sentences.simple: It must have been a terrible moment for the Witch. She suddenly saw that her power of turning people into dust, which had been quite real in her own world, was not going to work in ours.
sentences.grammar: 'Must have + past form' is a strong guess about the past; 'was not going to work' says what she found would not happen.
