sentences.context: she must not be allowed to go rampaging about the house
sentences.simple: No matter what happened, she must not be allowed to go rushing wildly about the house.
sentences.grammar: 'Must not be allowed to' means 'we must not let her'; 'Whatever happened' means 'no matter what'.

sentences.context: If he had heard that bit about the land of youth a few days ago he would have thought
sentences.simple: If Digory had heard about the land of youth a few days earlier, he would have thought Aunt Letty was just talking without meaning anything, as grown-ups do. It would not have interested him.
sentences.grammar: 'If + had heard, would have thought' talks about something that did not happen: he did not hear it then, so this is what would have happened.

sentences.context: if we’ve fallen down some diggings—as it might be for a new station on the Underground
sentences.simple: If we have fallen down some diggings, as it might be for a new station on the Underground, someone will come and get us out soon.
sentences.grammar: 'As it might be' gives an example (like 'for instance'); 'if we’ve fallen' is a real possibility, so the result uses 'will'.

sentences.context: he gave the sort of whinny a horse would give if, after years of being a cab-horse
sentences.simple: The horse made the kind of sound a horse would make if, after years of being a cab-horse, it found itself back in the old field where it had played as a young horse, and saw someone it remembered and loved coming across the field to bring it a lump of sugar.
sentences.grammar: 'Would give if ... found' is an imagined case; 'after years of being' is 'after + -ing'; 'had played' is earlier than 'found'.

sentences.context: She would have had her hands in Digory’s pocket before you could say knife
sentences.simple: She would have had her hands in Digory’s pocket before you could say knife, but Digory grabbed Polly and shouted out.
sentences.grammar: 'Would have had' shows what nearly happened but did not; 'before you could say knife' is an idiom for 'very quickly'.

sentences.context: You have not made the first joke; you have only been the first joke
sentences.simple: You have not made the first joke. You have only been the first joke.
sentences.grammar: 'Make a joke' (say something funny) is different from 'be a joke' (be the thing people laugh at); 'have not made / have been' is the present perfect.

sentences.context: you need not always be grave
sentences.simple: Now that you can speak and think, you do not always have to be serious.
sentences.grammar: 'Need not' means 'do not have to'; 'Now that' gives the reason.

sentences.context: And as Adam’s race has done the harm, Adam’s race shall help to heal it
sentences.simple: Adam’s race has done the harm, so Adam’s race will help to heal it.
sentences.grammar: 'As' here means 'because'; 'shall' is a strong promise or order that something will happen.

sentences.context: Are you ready to undo the wrong that you have done to my sweet country
sentences.simple: Are you ready to put right the wrong that you have done to my dear country of Narnia on the very day it began?
sentences.grammar: 'Ready to + verb' asks if he is willing to act; 'that you have done' (present perfect) tells which wrong, one that still matters now.

sentences.context: It would have been better if he had not
sentences.simple: It would have been better if Digory had not looked at the apple and smelled it.
sentences.grammar: 'Would have been better if he had not' talks about the past: he did it, and it was a mistake.

sentences.context: She was just throwing away the core of an apple which she had eaten
sentences.simple: She was just throwing away the core of an apple that she had eaten.
sentences.grammar: 'Was throwing' ('was + verb-ing') is the action in progress; 'had eaten' ('had + past form') happened before it.

sentences.context: that is why all the rest are now a horror to her
sentences.simple: That is the reason all the other apples are now a horror to her.
sentences.grammar: 'That is why' gives the reason for what was just said; 'all the rest' means all the other ones.

sentences.context: All get what they want; they do not always like it
sentences.simple: All people get what they want, but they do not always like it.
sentences.grammar: 'What they want' means 'the things that they want' and comes after 'get'; the semicolon joins two opposite ideas.

sentences.context: if ever they were sad or afraid or angry, the thought of all that golden goodness
sentences.simple: As long as they both lived, if they were ever sad or afraid or angry, the thought of all that golden goodness would come back and make them sure that all was well.
sentences.grammar: 'If ever' means 'whenever'; 'would come back' shows something that happened again and again; 'as long as' means 'for all the time that'.

sentences.context: there was a great storm all over the south of England which blew the tree down
sentences.simple: A great storm came all over the south of England, and it blew the tree down.
sentences.grammar: 'Which blew the tree down' tells more about the storm; 'blew down' is a verb + small word that means 'made fall by wind'.

sentences.context: a very old man with shaggy white hair which grew over most of his face
sentences.simple: He was a very old man with rough white hair, which grew over most of his face as well as on his head. The children liked him almost at once. But on the first evening, when he came out to meet them at the front door, he looked so odd that Lucy, who was the youngest, was a little afraid of him. Edmund, who was the next youngest, wanted to laugh. He had to keep on pretending that he was blowing his nose, to hide it.
sentences.grammar: ‘which grew over…’ is an extra part that tells more about the hair; ‘as well as’ means ‘and also’; ‘who was the youngest’ gives extra facts about Lucy.

sentences.context: We’ve fallen on our feet and no mistake
sentences.simple: We have been very lucky, and there is no doubt about it.
sentences.grammar: ‘have fallen on our feet’ is a saying that means ‘we have been lucky’; ‘and no mistake’ means ‘for sure’.

sentences.context: she knew that it is very foolish to shut oneself into any wardrobe
sentences.simple: She stepped into the wardrobe at once, got in among the coats and rubbed her face against them. She left the door open, of course, because she knew that it is very foolish to shut yourself into any wardrobe.
sentences.grammar: ‘oneself’ means ‘yourself’ or any person; ‘leaving the door open’ tells how she did it; ‘is’ stays in the present because it is always true.

sentences.context: if only I had worked harder at geography when I was a little Faun
sentences.simple: If only I had worked harder at geography when I was a little Faun, I would no doubt know all about those strange countries.
sentences.grammar: ‘if only + had worked’ is a wish about the past that did not happen; ‘should … know’ here means ‘would know’.

sentences.context: it is winter in Narnia, and has been for ever so long
sentences.simple: It is winter in Narnia, and it has been winter for a very long time. We will both catch cold if we stand here talking in the snow.
sentences.grammar: ‘has been’ joins a time in the past to now; ‘for ever so long’ means ‘for a very long time’; ‘shall’ here means ‘will’.

sentences.context: how would it be if you came and had tea with me?
sentences.simple: Daughter of Eve, from the far land of Spare Oom, where summer never ends around the bright city of War Drobe, would you like to come and have tea with me?
sentences.grammar: ‘how would it be if you came’ uses the past form to make a polite offer; it means ‘would you like to come?’.

sentences.context: I was to catch them and hand them over to her
sentences.simple: I had orders from the White Witch. If I ever saw a Son of Adam or a Daughter of Eve in the wood, I was to catch them and hand them over to her.
sentences.grammar: ‘was to + verb’ tells what someone had to do because of an order; ‘if ever I saw’ means ‘if I ever saw’.

sentences.context: He had expected to find her in a few seconds and was very surprised when he did not
sentences.simple: He had expected to find her in a few seconds, and he was very surprised when he did not.
sentences.grammar: ‘had expected’ (past perfect) is the earlier time, before ‘was surprised’; ‘when he did not’ means ‘when he did not find her’.

sentences.context: She could have made it up with the others quite easily at any moment
sentences.simple: She could easily have made it up with the others at any moment, if she had been able to make herself say that the whole thing was only a story made up for fun.
sentences.grammar: ‘could have + made’ tells what was possible in the past but did not happen; ‘made it up with’ means ‘became friends again’; ‘brought herself to’ means ‘made herself do something hard’.

sentences.context: for she knew, though Edmund did not, that this was enchanted Turkish Delight
sentences.simple: The Queen probably knew quite well what he was thinking. She knew, though Edmund did not, that this was enchanted Turkish Delight. Anyone who had once tasted it would want more and more of it, and, if they were allowed, would even go on eating it until they killed themselves.
sentences.grammar: ‘though Edmund did not’ adds a contrast, and ‘did not’ stands for ‘did not know’; ‘would want’ tells what always happened after one taste.

sentences.context: I might have to be very angry with you if you came alone
sentences.simple: I might have to be very angry with you if you came alone.
sentences.grammar: ‘might have to’ means ‘perhaps I will need to’; ‘if you came’ uses the past form for something that may happen, and it sounds softer.

sentences.context: does your experience lead you to regard your brother or your sister as the more reliable
sentences.simple: If you will excuse me for asking the question: from what you have seen, do you think your brother or your sister is the one you can trust more?
sentences.grammar: ‘lead you to regard A as B’ means ‘make you think of A as B’; ‘the more reliable’ compares two people and picks one.

sentences.context: I should not be at all surprised to find that the other world had a separate time of its own
sentences.simple: If there really is a door in this house that leads to some other world, and if she had got into that world, I should not be at all surprised to find that it had a separate time of its own. (This is a very strange house, and even I know very little about it.) So however long you stayed there, it would never take up any of our time.
sentences.grammar: ‘if … had got into’ talks about something that may be true; ‘should not be surprised to find that’ means ‘would not be surprised if I found that’; ‘so that’ gives the result.

sentences.context: He had just noticed a piece of paper which had been nailed through the carpet to the floor
sentences.simple: He had just noticed a piece of paper. Someone had put a nail through it, through the carpet and into the floor.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been nailed’ is passive past perfect: the nailing happened before he noticed, and the sentence does not say who did it.

sentences.context: Why shouldn’t it be leading us into a trap?
sentences.simple: It could well be leading us into a trap.
sentences.grammar: ‘Why shouldn’t it be …?’ is a question that really means ‘it could well be’; ‘be leading’ shows it is happening now.

sentences.context: I’d vote for going back and getting something from the larder
sentences.simple: I would vote for going back and getting something from the food store, but there does not seem to be any certainty of getting into this country again once you have got out of it.
sentences.grammar: ‘vote for + -ing’ means ‘say you want to do something’; ‘only’ here means ‘but’; ‘once you’ve got out’ means ‘after you have got out’.

sentences.context: None of the children knew who Aslan was any more than you do
sentences.simple: None of the children knew who Aslan was, just as you do not know. But the moment the Beaver had said these words, everyone felt quite different.
sentences.grammar: ‘none … any more than you do’ means you do not know either; ‘the moment (that)’ means ‘as soon as’.

sentences.context: in the dream it feels as if it had some enormous meaning
sentences.simple: Perhaps it has sometimes happened to you in a dream that someone says something you do not understand, but in the dream it feels as if it had some enormous meaning. The meaning may be a terrible one that turns the whole dream into a nightmare. Or it may be a lovely meaning, too lovely to put into words, which makes the dream so beautiful that you remember it all your life and always wish you could get into that dream again.
sentences.grammar: ‘as if + had’ uses the past form to talk about something that only seems true; ‘either … or else’ gives two kinds of meaning.

sentences.context: it’ll be the most she can do and more than I expect of her
sentences.simple: If she can stand on her two feet and look him in the face, that is the most she will be able to do, and it is more than I expect of her.
sentences.grammar: ‘the most she can do’ means her limit; ‘more than I expect of her’ means ‘more than I think she can do’; the ‘if’ part names something hard.

sentences.context: if there’s anyone who can appear before Aslan without their knees knocking
sentences.simple: If there is anyone who can stand in front of Aslan without their knees knocking, they are either braver than most or else just silly.
sentences.grammar: ‘their’ is used for one person (‘anyone’); ‘either … or else’ gives two choices; ‘knees knocking’ means knees shaking with fear.

sentences.context: He would never have found his way if the moon hadn’t come out
sentences.simple: He would never have found his way if the moon had not come out by the time he got to the other river. (You remember that, when they first arrived at the Beavers’, he had seen a smaller river flowing into the great one lower down.)
sentences.grammar: ‘would never have found … if … had not come out’ talks about the past: the moon did come out, so he did find his way.

sentences.context: he might have given up the whole plan and gone back and owned up
sentences.simple: In fact I really think he might have given up the whole plan, gone back, told the truth and made friends with the others, if he had not happened to say to himself, “When I’m King of Narnia the first thing I shall do will be to make some decent roads.”
sentences.grammar: ‘might have + given up’ tells what was possible in the past but did not happen; ‘if he hadn’t happened to say’ gives the reason it did not; ‘owned up’ means ‘told the truth’.

sentences.context: If you hadn’t all been in such a plaguey fuss when we were starting
sentences.simple: If you had not all been in such a fuss when we were starting, I would have brought some pillows,” said Mrs. Beaver.
sentences.grammar: ‘If + had been … I’d have brought’ talks about an unreal past: they were in a fuss, so she did not bring pillows.

sentences.context: It would have been a dreadful thing for the Beavers and the children if the night had remained fine
sentences.simple: It would have been a terrible thing for the Beavers and the children if the night had stayed fine. The wolves would then have been able to follow their trail, and ten to one would have caught them before they got to the cave.
sentences.grammar: ‘would have been … if + had remained’ talks about something that did not happen; ‘ten to one’ means ‘very likely’.

sentences.context: Unless you have looked at a world of snow as long as Edmund had been looking at it
sentences.simple: If you have not looked at a world of snow for as long as Edmund had been looking at it, you will hardly be able to imagine how good those green patches were after the endless white.
sentences.grammar: ‘Unless you have…’ means ‘if you have not…’; ‘had been looking’ is an action that went on up to an earlier past time; ‘hardly’ means ‘almost not’.

sentences.context: If it had not been so angry that it simply had to howl it would have got him by the throat at once
sentences.simple: If it had not been so angry that it simply had to howl, it would have got Peter by the throat at once.
sentences.grammar: ‘so angry that’ gives a result; ‘if it had not been … it would have got’ talks about an unreal past: it did howl, so it did not catch him.

sentences.context: He knows that unless I have blood as the Law says all Narnia will be overturned
sentences.simple: He knows that unless I have blood, as the Law says, all Narnia will be overturned and will be lost in fire and water.
sentences.grammar: ‘unless’ means ‘if not’; ‘as the Law says’ means ‘in the way the Law says’; ‘will be overturned’ is passive.

sentences.context: when a willing victim who had committed no treachery was killed in a traitor’s stead
sentences.simple: She would have known that when a willing victim who had not betrayed anyone was killed in the place of a traitor, the Table would crack and Death itself would start working backward.
sentences.grammar: ‘would have known’ means she did not know; ‘who had not betrayed anyone’ gives extra facts about the victim; ‘in a traitor’s stead’ means ‘in the place of a traitor’.

sentences.context: they might have left the body alone
sentences.simple: Oh, it is too bad. They could have left the body alone.
sentences.grammar: ‘might have + left’ means they could have done it but did not; here Lucy is sad and angry about it.

sentences.context: Once the feet are put right, all the rest of him will follow
sentences.simple: Once the feet are put right, all the rest of him will follow.
sentences.grammar: ‘Once + present’ means ‘as soon as’; ‘are put right’ is passive, so it does not say who does it.

sentences.context: It was the same day and the same hour of the day on which they had all gone into the wardrobe
sentences.simple: It was the same day and the same hour of the day when they had all gone into the wardrobe to hide.
sentences.grammar: ‘on which’ is a longer way to say ‘when’; ‘had gone’ is an earlier time than ‘was’.

sentences.context: I know not how it is, but this lamp on the post worketh upon me strangely
sentences.simple: I do not know how it is, but this lamp on the post has a strange effect on me.
sentences.grammar: Old-style speech: ‘I know not’ means ‘I do not know’, and ‘worketh’ means ‘works’; ‘strangely’ means ‘in a strange way’.

sentences.context: if ye will all have it so, let us go on and take the adventure that shall fall to us
sentences.simple: Then in the name of Aslan, if you will all have it so, let us go on and take the adventure that will come to us.
sentences.grammar: Old-style speech: ‘ye’ means ‘you’; ‘have it so’ means ‘want it that way’; ‘shall fall to us’ means ‘will come to us’.

sentences.context: never since we four were Kings and Queens in Narnia have we set our hands to any high matter
sentences.simple: Since we four were Kings and Queens in Narnia, we have never started any big job, such as battles, quests, great deeds of fighting, acts of justice and the like, and then given it up. Always, what we have taken in hand, we have finished.
sentences.grammar: ‘never’ at the start makes ‘have’ come before ‘we’ (‘have we set’); this is an old way to speak; ‘given over’ means ‘given up’.

sentences.context: Shasta, who had never learned that it is wrong to listen behind doors
sentences.simple: Shasta had never learned that it is wrong to listen behind doors. So he sat with his ear to a crack in the wall of the cottage to hear what the grown-ups said.
sentences.grammar: 'who had never learned' is a relative clause giving extra news about Shasta; 'had learned' (past perfect) looks back to a time before he sat down.

sentences.context: you'd better be lying dead tonight than go to be a human slave
sentences.simple: It would be better for you to be dead tonight than to go to his house tomorrow as a human slave.
sentences.grammar: 'had better X than Y' says X is the better choice than Y, so Y must be very bad.

sentences.context: as you and I would feel if we had just overheard our parents
sentences.simple: Do not think that Shasta felt as you and I would feel if we had just heard our parents talk about selling us for slaves.
sentences.grammar: 'would feel if we had just overheard' pictures an imagined case that is not real; 'must not imagine' tells the reader not to think so.

sentences.context: It would be dreadful to find, when I get back to Narnia
sentences.simple: It would be terrible to find, when I get back to Narnia, that I have picked up a lot of low, bad habits.
sentences.grammar: 'would be dreadful' is a worry about something that might be true; 'I've picked up' (present perfect) means he already has the habits, and 'pick up' means learn.

sentences.context: well, if that's not fishy, call me a cob
sentences.simple: A high-born Tarkheena rides alone at night in her brother's armor and wants no questions. If that is not strange, then call me a cob!
sentences.grammar: 'if that's not fishy, call me a cob' means 'I am sure it is fishy (strange and not honest)'; 'call me X' is a way to say 'I will be X if I am wrong'.

sentences.context: Everyone had been putting off this difficulty
sentences.simple: Everyone had been putting off this problem. But now they could not put it off any longer.
sentences.grammar: 'had been putting off' (past perfect continuous) shows they had done it for some time before; 'could be put off no longer' is a passive: nobody could wait any more.

sentences.context: one usually gets on better with people when one is making plans
sentences.simple: Aravis became a little less unfriendly to Shasta during these talks. People get on better when they make plans than when they talk about nothing in particular.
sentences.grammar: 'One' means 'a person in general' (formal); 'gets on better ... when ... than when ...' compares two times, and 'get on' means be friendly.

sentences.context: you would be happy, for in that land no maiden is forced to marry against her will
sentences.simple: If you were in Narnia you would be happy, because in that land no girl is forced to marry against her will.
sentences.grammar: 'If you were ... you would be' is an imagined case; 'is forced to marry' is a passive (someone makes her), and 'against her will' means she does not want it.

sentences.context: it would have been better if he had held his tongue
sentences.simple: It would have been better if Shasta had kept quiet. The soldier hit him on the side of the face and nearly knocked him down.
sentences.grammar: 'would have been better if he had held' is an unreal past case: he did not keep quiet; 'hold one's tongue' means stay silent.

sentences.context: everyone who is less important has to get out of the way for everyone who is more important
sentences.simple: In Tashbaan there is one rule for the traffic. Everyone who is less important has to get out of the way for everyone who is more important. If not, you get a cut from a whip or a punch from the end of a spear.
sentences.grammar: 'which is that ...' explains what the rule is; 'has to' means must; 'unless' means 'if not'.

sentences.context: could find it in your heart to show him so much favor
sentences.simple: I was surprised that you could ever be willing to show him so much favor.
sentences.grammar: 'it was a wonder to me that ...' is old, formal English for 'I was surprised that ...'; 'find it in your heart to' means be willing to.

sentences.context: Easily in but not easily out, as the lobster said in the lobster pot
sentences.simple: It is easy to get in but not easy to get out, as the lobster said in the lobster pot!
sentences.grammar: A short saying with the verb left out: 'easily in but not easily out' means easy to get in but not easy to get out; 'as ... said' gives the lobster's words as a joke.

sentences.context: Oh, if only I had never left Cair Paravel
sentences.simple: I wish I had never left Cair Paravel.
sentences.grammar: 'if only + had + past participle' is a wish about the past: she did leave, and it cannot be changed.

sentences.context: how would it be if your Majesties bade the Prince to a great banquet
sentences.simple: What if you asked the Prince to a great feast on board our own ship, the Splendor Hyaline, tomorrow night?
sentences.grammar: 'how would it be if ...?' is an old way to suggest an idea ('what if ...?'); 'bade' is the past of 'bid', here meaning 'asked'.

sentences.context: If they knew I wasn't one of themselves, they'd never let me out of this house alive
sentences.simple: If they knew I was not one of them, they would never let me leave this house alive.
sentences.grammar: 'If + past (knew), would + verb' pictures an imagined case: they do not know now, but this is what would follow if they did.

sentences.context: there is a great difference between a noise heard letting you in with your friends
sentences.simple: A noise in the morning that lets you in with your friends is very different from a noise at nightfall that shuts you out when you are alone.
sentences.grammar: 'a noise heard ...' uses a past participle to mean 'a noise that is heard'; 'letting you in' and 'shutting you out' say what each noise does.

sentences.context: if he had read as many books as you have about journeys over deserts
sentences.simple: It was a crazy idea. If Shasta had read as many books as you have about journeys over deserts, he would never have thought of it.
sentences.grammar: 'If he had read ..., he would never have dreamed' is an unreal past case: he had read no books, so he did dream of it.

sentences.context: If you had given me the swiftest of the galleys at sunrise
sentences.simple: If you had given me the fastest ship at sunrise, when I first saw the ship of the barbarians was gone, I might have caught them.
sentences.grammar: 'If you had given ..., I would perhaps have overtaken' is an unreal past case: the Tisroc did not give the ship, so Rabadash did not catch them.

sentences.context: I am determined not to put my hand out farther than I can draw it back
sentences.simple: I have firmly decided not to put my hand out farther than I can pull it back.
sentences.grammar: 'determined not to + verb' means firmly decided not to; 'farther than I can draw it back' is a picture: do not reach out more than you can pull back.

sentences.context: He had better cool his blood abroad than boil it in inaction here
sentences.simple: It is better for him to cool his blood in another country than to boil it here doing nothing.
sentences.grammar: 'had better X than Y' means X is the wiser choice than Y; 'cool his blood' and 'boil it' are pictures for becoming calm and for staying angry.

sentences.context: Shasta would nearly have fallen asleep if he had not had to dismount
sentences.simple: Shasta would almost have fallen asleep if he had not had to get off and walk now and then.
sentences.grammar: 'would nearly have fallen asleep if he had not had to' is an unreal past case: he had to walk, so he did not fall asleep.

sentences.context: He had not yet learned that if you do one good deed
sentences.simple: Shasta did not yet know this: when you do one good thing, you are usually given another, harder and better thing to do.
sentences.grammar: 'had not yet learned' (past perfect) means he did not know it before then; 'is to be set to do' is a passive meaning 'is given a job to do'.

sentences.context: have yet little knowledge of things future
sentences.simple: I know many things that are happening now by my art, but I still know little about things in the future.
sentences.grammar: 'things future' puts the adjective after the noun (old style, 'future things'); 'yet' here means 'still'.

sentences.context: If the horse had been any good—or if he had known how to get any good out of the horse
sentences.simple: If the horse had been any good, or if Shasta had known how to get any use out of it, he would have risked a wild gallop. But he knew he could not make that horse gallop.
sentences.grammar: 'If ... had been ..., he would have risked' is an unreal past case; 'any good' means at all good, and 'get good out of' means get some use from.

sentences.context: somebody ought to tell someone about it with a view to doing something
sentences.simple: The Rabbit agreed that this was very surprising news. He said somebody ought to tell someone, so that something could be done.
sentences.grammar: 'with a view to + -ing' means 'with the aim of doing'; 'ought to' means should.

sentences.context: But if you would not be taken for one, another time try not to hear what's meant for other ears
sentences.simple: If you do not want people to think you are a traitor, next time try not to hear what was not meant for you.
sentences.grammar: 'taken for' means thought to be; 'if you would not be ...' means 'if you do not want to be ...'; 'what's meant for other ears' means words said for other people.

sentences.context: He would have been wiser if he had set his men to making ladders
sentences.simple: He would have been wiser if he had told his men to make ladders. But that takes too long, and he cannot wait.
sentences.grammar: 'would have been wiser if he had set' is an unreal past case; 'set his men to making' means gave his men the job of making.

sentences.context: He ought to have ridden back to Tashbaan as soon as the first attack failed
sentences.simple: He should have ridden back to Tashbaan as soon as the first attack failed, because his whole plan needed speed and surprise.
sentences.grammar: 'ought to have + past participle' says what was right to do in the past but was not done.

sentences.context: His Highness would not be your son if he did not inherit your conditions
sentences.simple: His Highness would not be your son if he did not have your nature.
sentences.grammar: 'would not be ... if he did not' is an imagined case; 'conditions' is an old word here meaning a person's nature.

sentences.context: I'd be just as pleased—or very nearly—at finding he's my father even if he weren't a king
sentences.simple: I would be almost as happy to find he is my father even if he were not a king.
sentences.grammar: 'even if he weren't' uses 'were' for an imagined case; 'pleased at finding' is a preposition followed by -ing.

sentences.context: Do not dare not to dare
sentences.simple: Do not be afraid to be bold.
sentences.grammar: 'Do not dare not to dare' is a word play: 'dare' means have the courage, so it means 'do not be afraid to be bold'.

sentences.context: Hast no more power to start away from thy crown than any sentry from his post
sentences.simple: You have no more power to leave your crown than a guard has to leave his place.
sentences.grammar: Old English: 'hast' is 'have' and 'thy' is 'your'; 'no more ... than' means 'just as little as'.

sentences.context: what Rabadash hadn't realized is that it is very easy to frighten people who know
sentences.simple: Rabadash had not seen that it is easy to frighten people who know you can have them boiled alive as soon as you say so.
sentences.grammar: 'what Rabadash hadn't realized' is a noun clause that is the subject; 'hadn't realized' (past perfect) looks back from the time of the scene.

sentences.context: At any rate, no one noticed that they had ever been away
sentences.simple: In any case, nobody noticed that they had ever been away, and they never told anyone except one very wise grown-up.
sentences.grammar: ‘had ever been away’ is the past perfect: it looks back to a time before the story time; ‘at any rate’ means ‘in any case’.

sentences.context: it all seemed to have taken no time at all
sentences.simple: While they were in Narnia, it seemed they ruled for years and years. But when they came back through the door and were in England again, it seemed that none of it had taken any time.
sentences.grammar: ‘seemed to have taken’ means ‘looked as if it had already taken’: ‘seem to have’ + the past form talks about something already finished.

sentences.context: Edmund had put down his coat on the station seat just before the magic overtook them
sentences.simple: Edmund had put his coat down on the station seat just before the magic caught them, so he and Peter took turns to carry Peter’s greatcoat.
sentences.grammar: ‘had put down’ is the past perfect: it happened before the other past action, ‘overtook’; ‘took it in turns’ means one person after another.

sentences.context: Anyone would think you had forgotten that we ourselves were once Kings and Queens
sentences.simple: It looks as if you have forgotten that we ourselves were once Kings and Queens, and sat on a dais just like that in our great hall.
sentences.grammar: ‘Anyone would think you had …’ means ‘it looks as if you had …’; ‘had forgotten’ is the past perfect.

sentences.context: If you had been there you would have heard them saying things like
sentences.simple: If you had been there, you would have heard them saying things like this.
sentences.grammar: ‘If + past perfect, would have + past form’ talks about something that did not happen: you were not there, so you did not hear.

sentences.context: unless they had realized where they were and remembered most of the things, they would hardly have known they were treasures
sentences.simple: The treasures were so covered with dust that they would hardly have known these were treasures if they had not understood where they were and remembered most of the things.
sentences.grammar: ‘unless + past perfect, would have + past form’: ‘unless’ means ‘if not’, and the sentence tells what would have happened if it had not been so.

sentences.context: It was indeed a shattering loss; for this was an enchanted horn
sentences.simple: It was a terrible loss, because this was a magic horn. Whenever you blew it, help was sure to come to you, wherever you were.
sentences.grammar: ‘for’ here means ‘because’; ‘whenever’ means ‘every time that’; ‘was certain to come’ means ‘would surely come’.

sentences.context: Why shouldn’t hundreds of years have gone past in Narnia while only one year has passed for us
sentences.simple: Why can it not be that hundreds of years have gone by in Narnia while only one year has gone by for us in England?
sentences.grammar: ‘Why shouldn’t … have gone’ asks why something is not possible; ‘should not have’ + past form is a guess about the past; ‘while’ links two things at the same time.

sentences.context: though one meets bad Dwarfs, I never heard of a Dwarf who was a fool
sentences.simple: The Dwarf was a very able person. One meets bad Dwarfs, but I never heard of a Dwarf who was a fool. He cut the fish open, cleaned them, and said:
sentences.grammar: ‘though’ means ‘although’; ‘one meets’ means ‘a person meets’ (here, ‘you meet’); the brackets hold the writer’s own comment.

sentences.context: Can you lay your hand on your hearts and tell me I’m really alive
sentences.simple: Can you put your hand on your hearts and tell me I am really alive?
sentences.grammar: ‘Can you … and tell me’ asks them to do two things; ‘lay your hand on your heart’ means to promise that something is true.

sentences.context: if Caspian had been a very little older, the tone of his uncle’s voice would have warned him
sentences.simple: If Caspian had been a very little older, the sound of his uncle’s voice would have warned him that it was wiser to be quiet.
sentences.grammar: ‘If + past perfect, would have + past form’ talks about something that did not happen: Caspian was not older, so he was not warned.

sentences.context: It was your Highness’s ancestor, Caspian the First,” said Doctor Cornelius, “who first conquered Narnia
sentences.simple: It was your ancestor, Caspian the First, who first won Narnia in war and made it his kingdom.
sentences.grammar: ‘It was … who …’ puts the person first to stress that he, and no one else, did the action.

sentences.context: Whom, not who, your Highness
sentences.simple: It should be ‘whom’, not ‘who’, your Highness.
sentences.grammar: ‘whom’ is the form for the person who receives the action (conquered whom?), while ‘who’ is for the person who does it.

sentences.context: You have seen what no man now alive has seen, nor will see again
sentences.simple: You have seen something that no man now alive has seen, and that no man will see again.
sentences.grammar: ‘nor will see again’ means ‘and will not see again’: ‘nor’ adds a second negative idea; ‘what’ means ‘the thing that’.

sentences.context: until you got to know him really well, it was hard to know when he was joking
sentences.simple: His voice was serious and his eyes were happy, so until you got to know him really well, it was hard to tell when he was joking and when he was serious.
sentences.grammar: ‘get to know’ means to come to know someone little by little; ‘until’ gives the time up to which it was hard to tell.

sentences.context: I wonder you have never asked me before,” said the Doctor, “why, being the son of King Caspian
sentences.simple: I am surprised that you have never asked me before why, being the son of King Caspian, you are not King Caspian yourself.
sentences.grammar: ‘being the son of King Caspian’ is a short phrase that gives a reason, like ‘because you are the son’; ‘I wonder you have never asked’ means ‘it surprises me that you have never asked’.

sentences.context: as long as he was in country that he knew, but afterward he kept to the high road
sentences.simple: All night he rode south. While he was in country he knew, he chose side roads and horse paths through woods, but afterward he kept to the high road.
sentences.grammar: ‘as long as’ here means ‘for the time that’; ‘kept to’ means ‘stayed on’; ‘but afterward’ shows the change.

sentences.context: he knew that his life hung by a thread during the wild career that followed
sentences.simple: He stayed on the horse, but he knew his life hung by a thread during the wild ride that followed.
sentences.grammar: ‘hung by a thread’ is an idiom: he was very close to death; ‘career’ here means a fast, wild run.

sentences.context: We ought to have killed it at once, or else let it alone
sentences.simple: We should have killed it at once, or else left it alone.
sentences.grammar: ‘ought to have’ + past form says what was the right thing to do in the past, but it was not done; ‘or else’ gives the other choice.

sentences.context: if his claws and teeth could not keep his skin whole, it wasn’t worth keeping
sentences.simple: The Badger could have had the same if he had liked, but he said he was a beast. If his claws and teeth could not keep his skin unhurt, it was not worth keeping.
sentences.grammar: ‘wasn’t worth keeping’ means ‘was not good enough to keep’; ‘If … could not’ sets a condition; ‘could have had … if he had liked’ is a past case that did not happen.

sentences.context: They had some vague idea, perhaps, of an occasional raid on some Human farmstead
sentences.simple: Perhaps they had an unclear idea of sometimes attacking a Human farm, or of attacking a group of hunters if it went too far into these wild southern lands.
sentences.grammar: ‘idea of’ tells what the idea was about; ‘it’ stands for ‘the party of hunters’; ‘if’ gives the case when they would attack.

sentences.context: And as so often happens, the enemy turned out stronger than they had reckoned
sentences.simple: As so often happens, it turned out that the enemy was stronger than they had thought.
sentences.grammar: ‘turned out’ + describing word means ‘proved to be’; ‘than they had reckoned’ uses the past perfect to compare with what they had thought before.

sentences.context: He, with most of the Dwarfs, was to have fallen on the King’s right wing at daybreak
sentences.simple: He, with most of the Dwarfs, was to have attacked the King’s right wing at daybreak. Then, when they were fighting hard, Giant Wimbleweather, with the Centaurs and some of the fiercest animals, was to have broken out from another place and tried to cut the King’s right wing off from the rest of the army.
sentences.grammar: ‘was to have’ + past form tells of a plan made before; the story then shows it did not work.

sentences.context: I might as well die on a wild goose chase as die here
sentences.simple: I might just as well die on a useless search as die here.
sentences.grammar: ‘might as well … as …’ says one choice is as good as the other; ‘wild goose chase’ is an idiom for a useless search.

sentences.context: I’d been plugging away for many hours when there came a sound that I’d never heard the like of
sentences.simple: I had been working hard for many hours when I heard a sound like nothing I had ever heard in all my life.
sentences.grammar: ‘I’d been plugging’ is ‘I had been plugging’ (past perfect continuous): it was going on until a later past moment; ‘never heard the like of’ means ‘never heard anything like’.

sentences.context: Kids like us don’t often have the chance of meeting a great warrior like you
sentences.simple: Young people like us do not often get the chance to meet a great fighter like you.
sentences.grammar: ‘have the chance of meeting’ means ‘get the chance to meet’; ‘Kids like us’ means ‘kids of our kind’.

sentences.context: she would have flown at Trumpkin, if Peter had not laid his hand on her arm
sentences.simple: Lucy went deep red, and I think she would have jumped at Trumpkin if Peter had not laid his hand on her arm.
sentences.grammar: ‘would have + past form, if + past perfect’ says what nearly happened but did not: Peter stopped her; ‘I think’ shows the writer is not sure.

sentences.context: I know Lucy may be right after all, but I can’t help it
sentences.simple: I know Lucy may be right after all, but I can’t do anything different.
sentences.grammar: ‘can’t help it’ means ‘cannot do anything else’; ‘may be right’ means ‘it is possible’; ‘after all’ means ‘in the end’.

sentences.context: You can’t help feeling stronger when you look at a place where you won a glorious victory
sentences.simple: When you look at a place where you won a great victory, and a kingdom too, hundreds of years ago, you cannot stop yourself from feeling stronger.
sentences.grammar: ‘can’t help feeling’ means ‘cannot stop yourself from feeling’; ‘not to mention’ adds one more thing.

sentences.context: Of course, if the children had attempted a journey like this a few days ago in England, they would have been knocked up
sentences.simple: If the children had tried a journey like this a few days ago in England, they would have been very tired.
sentences.grammar: ‘if + past perfect, would have been’ talks about something that did not happen; ‘knocked up’ is British for ‘very tired’.

sentences.context: The others had only Lucy’s directions to guide them, for Aslan was not only invisible to them but silent as well
sentences.simple: The others had only Lucy’s directions to guide them, because Aslan was not only invisible to them but silent as well.
sentences.grammar: ‘not only … but … as well’ joins two facts; ‘for’ here means ‘because’.

sentences.context: I could have, if I’d let myself
sentences.simple: I could have believed it, if I had let myself.
sentences.grammar: ‘could have’ stands for ‘could have believed’; ‘if I’d let myself’ is ‘if I had let myself’ (past perfect): it did not happen.

sentences.context: Have you forgotten that Miraz fell upon us almost before Trumpkin had gone
sentences.simple: Have you forgotten that Miraz attacked us almost before Trumpkin had gone, and that we were fighting for our lives for three hours and more?
sentences.grammar: ‘fell upon’ means ‘attacked’; ‘before Trumpkin had gone’ uses the past perfect for the earlier action.

sentences.context: I haven’t come to take your place, you know, but to put you into it
sentences.simple: I have not come to take your place, you know, but to put you into it.
sentences.grammar: ‘not … but …’ puts two aims side by side; ‘to’ + the base form says why he came.

sentences.context: For to prevent the effusion of blood, and for the avoiding of all other inconveniences
sentences.simple: To stop blood from being spilled and to avoid other trouble from the wars now in our land of Narnia, I choose to risk my own life for my trusted and loved Caspian in a fair fight. I will prove on your body that Caspian is the lawful King under me in Narnia, by my gift and by the laws of the Telmarines. I will also prove that you are twice guilty of treachery, for keeping Narnia from Caspian and for the hateful, bloody and unnatural murder of your kind lord and brother, King Caspian the Ninth.
sentences.grammar: Old letter style: ‘for to prevent’ and ‘for the avoiding of’ both mean ‘in order to avoid’; ‘it is our pleasure to’ means ‘we choose to’.

sentences.context: I knew he’d do it if he were properly chafed
sentences.simple: I knew he would do it if he were made really angry.
sentences.grammar: ‘if he were’ is used for an imagined case, with ‘would’ in the main part (‘he’d’ = ‘he would’).

sentences.context: I have a chance if I can keep him on the hop till his weight and short wind come against him
sentences.simple: I have a chance if I can keep him moving about until his weight and his short breath work against him, in this hot sun too.
sentences.grammar: ‘keep him on the hop’ is an idiom: keep him busy moving about; ‘short wind’ means he gets out of breath; ‘till’ means ‘until’.

sentences.context: If he fell, the mice finished him off; if he did not, someone else did.
sentences.simple: If he fell, the mice killed him. If he did not fall, someone else killed him.
sentences.grammar: ‘if he did not, someone else did’ leaves words out: ‘did’ stands for ‘finished him off’, so they are not said twice.

sentences.context: If you had felt yourself sufficient, it would have been a proof that you were not
sentences.simple: If you had felt that you were good enough, that would have been a proof that you were not.
sentences.grammar: ‘if + past perfect, would have been’ says what would have happened but did not; ‘sufficient’ means ‘good enough’.

sentences.context: known that you could be no true King of Narnia unless
sentences.simple: Sir Caspian, you could have known that you could be no true King of Narnia unless, like the kings of old, you were a son of Adam and came from the world of Adam’s sons.
sentences.grammar: ‘might have known’ means ‘had the chance to know, but did not’; ‘no true King … unless’ means ‘a true King only if’.

sentences.context: Nice fools we’d look on the platform of an English station in these.
sentences.simple: We would look like fools on the platform of an English station in these.
sentences.grammar: ‘Nice fools we’d look’ is a joke way to say ‘we would look like fools’; ‘nice’ is used to mean the opposite.

sentences.context: Last year, when he had been staying with the Pevensies
sentences.simple: Last year he stayed with the Pevensies. At that time he managed to hear them all talk about Narnia, and he loved to tease them about it.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been staying’ (past perfect continuous) is a stay that was already in the past before the story’s ‘now’; ‘when’ tells the time.

sentences.context: she couldn’t get rid of it because it had been a wedding present
sentences.simple: Aunt Alberta did not like the picture. But she could not get rid of it, because someone she did not want to upset had given it to her when she was married.
sentences.grammar: ‘it had been a wedding present’ is past perfect: it gives the reason, which came before ‘she couldn’t get rid of it’.

sentences.context: At the same moment an exercise book which had been lying beside Edmund
sentences.simple: At the same moment, a school book that had been lying next to Edmund on the bed moved. It rose and flew across the room to the wall behind him. Lucy felt her hair whipping round her face.
sentences.grammar: ‘which had been lying’ is a relative clause in the past perfect continuous: the book was lying there before it rose.

sentences.context: which Narnia had owned when Lucy and Edmund had reigned there
sentences.simple: The Dawn Treader was small next to the big ships that Narnia had owned when Lucy and Edmund ruled there.
sentences.grammar: ‘which Narnia had owned’ is a relative clause about the ships; ‘had owned’ and ‘had reigned’ are past perfect because that time was before the voyage.

sentences.context: Why exactly Eustace had slipped and reeled and stumbled all the way forward
sentences.simple: I never heard why Eustace had slipped and stumbled all the way to the front of the ship. He did not yet walk well on a ship.
sentences.grammar: The ‘Why exactly ...’ clause is the object of ‘heard’ and is put first; inside it the word order is normal (‘Eustace had slipped’), not a question.

sentences.context: if once I established peace in Narnia, I would sail east myself
sentences.simple: On the day he became king, Caspian made a promise. He said that when there was peace in Narnia, he would sail east for a year and a day to find his father’s friends.
sentences.grammar: ‘would sail’ is ‘will sail’ seen from the past: it says what he promised then; ‘if once I established peace’ means ‘as soon as I had made peace’.

sentences.context: Oars were used only when wind failed or for getting in
sentences.simple: People used the oars only when there was no wind, or to take the ship in and out of the harbor.
sentences.grammar: ‘Oars were used’ is passive: it tells what was done to the oars, not who used them; ‘for getting in’ is ‘for’ plus an -ing word.

sentences.context: If Caspian had been as experienced then as he became later on
sentences.simple: Caspian was not as experienced then as he later became. If he had been, he would not have made this suggestion. But at that time it seemed a very good one.
sentences.grammar: ‘If + past perfect, would have + verb’ talks about something that did not happen: he was not experienced, so he made the mistake.

sentences.context: But hardly had they raised their cups to their lips
sentences.simple: They had only just lifted their cups to their lips when the black-haired man nodded to his men.
sentences.grammar: ‘hardly had they raised’ is inversion: after ‘hardly’ at the start, ‘had’ comes before ‘they’; it means ‘they had just raised ... when’ the next thing happened.

sentences.context: where they found many other unfortunate prisoners; for Pug was of course a pirate
sentences.simple: They were taken to a long, rather dark place on the slave-ship. There they found many other unlucky prisoners, because Pug was a pirate.
sentences.grammar: ‘where they found ...’ is a clause about the place; ‘for’ here means ‘because’ and gives the reason.

sentences.context: and wondered what was happening to Caspian and tried to stop Eustace talking
sentences.simple: They sat in the straw. They wondered what was happening to Caspian. They tried to stop Eustace from talking as if everyone but him was wrong.
sentences.grammar: ‘was happening’ is the past continuous for something going on at that time; ‘what ...’ is an indirect question, so the word order is normal; ‘stop Eustace talking’ is ‘stop + person + -ing’.

sentences.context: At first, the only people who cheered were those who had been warned
sentences.simple: At first the only people who cheered were the ones that Bern’s messenger had told. They knew what was happening, and they wanted it to happen.
sentences.grammar: ‘those who had been warned’ is a ‘who’ clause in the passive past perfect: they were warned earlier, by someone else.

sentences.context: Had he known that Caspian had only one ship and one ship’s company
sentences.simple: If he had known that Caspian had only one ship and its crew, he would have spoken softly for the moment.
sentences.grammar: ‘Had he known’ means ‘If he had known’ (inversion, no ‘if’); it talks about something that was not true.

sentences.context: Bern could only tell them that he had seen his six companions sail away
sentences.simple: If Gumpas had known that Caspian had only one ship and its crew, he would have spoken softly for the moment.
sentences.grammar: ‘Had he known’ means ‘If he had known’ (inversion, no ‘if’); it is about the past and about something that was not true.

sentences.context: the old Eustace, Harold and Alberta’s Eustace, would have given up the climb
sentences.simple: The old Eustace would have stopped climbing after about ten minutes. But this Eustace did not.
sentences.grammar: ‘would have given up’ says what the old Eustace would have done; it did not happen, because he was now different.

sentences.context: Perhaps they had let him wander away on purpose simply
sentences.simple: Maybe the others had let him walk away on purpose, just so they could leave him behind.
sentences.grammar: ‘Perhaps they had let’ uses the past perfect for a guess about something earlier; ‘in order to’ gives the aim.

sentences.context: The dragon-that-had-been-Eustace held out its sore leg gladly enough
sentences.simple: The dragon that had once been Eustace held out its sore leg, and was glad enough to do it. It remembered how Lucy’s cordial had cured him of seasickness before he became a dragon.
sentences.grammar: ‘dragon-that-had-been-Eustace’ is a whole phrase joined with hyphens to work like one name; ‘had been’ and ‘had cured’ are past perfect for things before that time.

sentences.context: Eustace (unlike most boys) had never thought much of treasure
sentences.simple: Unlike most boys, Eustace had never cared much about treasure. But now he saw at once how useful it would be in this new world, which he had walked into by mistake through the picture.
sentences.grammar: ‘had never thought much of’ (past perfect) means that before then he had not valued treasure; the brackets (unlike most boys) add a small extra remark.

sentences.context: that one which was dead at about three o’clock that afternoon
sentences.simple: They tried to feel better. Everyone told everyone else that there were not likely to be more dragons. The dragon they saw was dead at about three o’clock that afternoon. So it could hardly have been killing people only a few hours before.
sentences.grammar: ‘would hardly have been killing’: ‘would have + past participle’ is a guess about the past, and ‘hardly’ makes it very unlikely that it was killing people hours before.

sentences.context: The bracelet which had fitted very nicely on the upper arm of a boy
sentences.simple: The bracelet had fitted well on a boy’s arm. It was much too small for the thick leg of a dragon.
sentences.grammar: ‘which had fitted’ is a ‘which’ clause in the past perfect; it tells us how the bracelet was before Eustace changed.

sentences.context: since the first day he came on board he had been an unmitigated nuisance
sentences.simple: Eustace saw more and more clearly that he had been a big trouble to everyone since his first day on the ship. He saw that now he was even more trouble.
sentences.grammar: ‘he had been’ (past perfect) looks back from the moment he understood; ‘since’ marks the starting time.

sentences.context: He was a very humane killer too, for he could dispatch a beast
sentences.simple: He was also a kind killer. He could kill an animal with one blow of his tail, so that it did not know it had been killed.
sentences.grammar: ‘so that it didn’t know’ gives the result; ‘it had been killed’ is a passive past perfect: the killing was already done.

sentences.context: instead of pursuing the ship it turned its head round
sentences.simple: The animal was very stupid. It did not follow the ship. It turned its head and sniffed along its own body, as if it hoped to find the Dawn Treader there.
sentences.grammar: ‘instead of + -ing’ means ‘not doing X, but doing Y’; ‘as if it expected’ tells what the animal seemed to think.

sentences.context: If it had been a hot day, no doubt some would have been tempted
sentences.simple: It was not a hot day. If it had been hot, some of them would have wanted to swim, and everyone would have had a drink.
sentences.grammar: ‘If + had been ..., would have been tempted’ (passive) is about a past that was not real: it was not a hot day.

sentences.context: we wouldn’t let them go away alive unless they’d done the needful for us
sentences.simple: We would not let the strangers go away alive, unless they had done what we needed.
sentences.grammar: ‘unless’ means ‘if not’; ‘they’d done’ is the past perfect (‘they had done’) for something that must be finished first.

sentences.context: more than one doubted whether Lucy had not merely imagined
sentences.simple: When they saw the boat and the empty sand, more than one of them wondered if Lucy had only imagined everything she told them.
sentences.grammar: ‘doubted whether Lucy had not merely imagined’: the ‘not’ does not make it negative; it means they thought she might have only imagined it. ‘all she had told them’ has no ‘that’.

sentences.context: she remembered what she had been told about the Magician walking
sentences.simple: She remembered what people had told her about the Magician. He walked on bare feet and made no more noise than a cat.
sentences.grammar: ‘what she had been told’ is a passive past perfect noun clause: it means ‘the things that someone had told her’.

sentences.context: where she felt quite sure there had been no picture before
sentences.simple: In the middle of the writing, where she felt quite sure there had been no picture before, she saw the great face of Aslan. He was staring into hers.
sentences.grammar: ‘where’ starts a clause about the place; ‘there had been no picture’ (past perfect) compares it with earlier.

sentences.context: Of course I could turn him into something else, or even put a spell
sentences.simple: Of course I could turn him into something else. Or I could put a spell on him so that they would not believe a word he said.
sentences.grammar: ‘could’ says what was possible; ‘a spell ... which would make them not believe’ is a relative clause about the spell, and ‘would make’ is its result.

sentences.context: which were so widely opened that he seemed to have no eyelids at all
sentences.simple: You noticed his eyes most. They were so wide open that he seemed to have no eyelids. He stared as if he was in terrible fear.
sentences.grammar: ‘so ... that ...’ shows a result; ‘which’ adds more information about his eyes.

sentences.context: there was set out such a banquet as had never been seen
sentences.simple: On the table there was a great feast. No one had ever seen such a feast, not even when Peter the High King kept his court at Cair Paravel.
sentences.grammar: ‘such a banquet as had never been seen’: ‘such ... as’ means ‘of the kind that’; ‘had never been seen’ is a passive past perfect, so it compares with every feast before.

sentences.context: while they had been talking the stars had grown fainter
sentences.simple: They could see it better now. While they were talking, the stars had become fainter, and big gaps of white light were opening in the east.
sentences.grammar: ‘while they had been talking’ (past perfect continuous) is the time before they saw the sky; ‘had grown fainter’ is the change that happened during it.

sentences.context: whether the sun at its rising did not look bigger in these seas
sentences.simple: Once or twice before, the Narnians had wondered if the sun looked bigger in these seas than it had at home.
sentences.grammar: ‘wondered whether ...’ starts an indirect question; ‘did not look bigger’ here just means ‘looked bigger’; ‘than it had looked’ (past perfect) compares with earlier times at home.

sentences.context: They could not have seen even the sun if their eyes
sentences.simple: They could not have looked even at the sun if the water of the Last Sea had not made their eyes strong.
sentences.grammar: ‘could not have seen ... if ... had not been strengthened’ (passive) is about the past: the water did make their eyes strong.

sentences.context: and if their eyes had not by now grown as strong as eagles’
sentences.simple: This last sea looked very like the Arctic. If their eyes had not become as strong as an eagle’s, the sun on all that white would have been too bright to bear.
sentences.grammar: ‘if ... had not grown, ... would have been unbearable’ is a past ‘if’ sentence: their eyes did grow strong, so it was not too bright.

sentences.context: back in our own world everyone soon started saying how Eustace had improved
sentences.simple: Back in our own world, everyone soon said that Eustace had got better. Only Aunt Alberta said he had become ordinary and annoying.
sentences.grammar: ‘how Eustace had improved’ is a noun clause with the past perfect: the change came before the people spoke.

sentences.context: Nobody asked you to come barging in, did they?
sentences.simple: No one asked you to push in like that, did they?
sentences.grammar: ‘did they?’ is a tag question: after a negative sentence (‘Nobody asked’) it takes a positive tag, and Jill does not want an answer, she wants him to agree he was wrong to come.

sentences.context: The voice had been growing softer toward the end of this speech
sentences.simple: The voice had been getting softer toward the end of this speech, and now it was gone.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been growing’ (past perfect continuous) says the change went on up to ‘now’ in the story, when the voice ‘faded away’.

sentences.context: She had been setting her teeth and clenching her fists for a terrible blast
sentences.simple: She had been holding her teeth together and making her hands into fists for a terrible blast of the Lion’s breath. But the breath had been so gentle that she did not even notice when she left the ground.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been setting … for’ (past perfect continuous) shows she had been getting ready before she looked back; ‘so gentle that’ shows the result.

sentences.context: ought to have been expecting, but which came as a surprise and a shock
sentences.simple: She came out lower than she went in. As soon as she did, she noticed something that she should have expected, but it still came as a surprise and a shock.
sentences.grammar: ‘ought to have been expecting’ means she should have expected it, but did not; the two ‘which’ clauses give two facts about the same thing.

sentences.context: It never occurred to Jill to disbelieve the Lion
sentences.simple: Jill never thought of not believing the Lion. No one who had seen his stern face could do that. And her mind suddenly made itself up.
sentences.grammar: ‘It occurred to Jill to + verb’ means the idea came to her; with ‘never’ it means she had no doubt; the dashes add a reason.

sentences.context: The sun which had been high overhead when she began her journey
sentences.simple: The sun had been high above her when she began her trip. Now it was getting into her eyes.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been’ (past perfect) shows the earlier time when the sun was high; ‘now getting’ shows the later time; ‘which’ adds more about the sun.

sentences.context: A little Faun who had been standing quietly beside the Dwarf
sentences.simple: A little Faun had been standing quietly beside the Dwarf’s elbow all this time. Now he handed the Dwarf a silver ear-trumpet.
sentences.grammar: ‘who had been standing’ (past perfect continuous) shows what the Faun was doing before he handed over the trumpet; ‘now handed’ is the new action.

sentences.context: It was made like the musical instrument called a serpent
sentences.simple: It was made like the musical instrument called a serpent, so that the tube went right round the Dwarf’s neck.
sentences.grammar: ‘It was made’ is passive (who made it is not said); ‘so that’ tells the result of the shape.

sentences.context: who was just gathering up the reins of his donkey
sentences.simple: Before she had time to ask any questions, they had reached the Dwarf. He was just taking up the reins of his donkey, ready to drive back to the castle.
sentences.grammar: ‘who was just gathering’ (past continuous) shows he was in the middle of the action when they came; ‘before she had time to’ shows she had no time.

sentences.context: whom everyone is a little afraid of and everyone makes fun of
sentences.simple: The Narnians felt about Trumpkin as people at school feel about an old teacher who is not kind. Everyone is a little afraid of him and makes fun of him, but nobody really dislikes him.
sentences.grammar: One ‘whom’ clause covers three actions (afraid of, makes fun of, dislikes); ‘of’ stays at the end, so ‘afraid of whom’ becomes ‘whom … afraid of’.

sentences.context: She had been a great lady, wise and gracious and happy
sentences.simple: She had been a great lady, wise and kind and happy. She was King Caspian’s bride, whom he had brought home from the east end of the world.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been’ and ‘had brought’ (past perfect) look back at her life before the story’s time; ‘whom he had brought’ adds more about the bride.

sentences.context: that the parliament had been going on quite long enough
sentences.simple: One or two owls added that even here in the ruined tower it was not nearly so dark as when they began, and that the meeting had gone on long enough.
sentences.grammar: After ‘added that’ the speech moves back one tense: ‘had been going on’ (past perfect continuous) says the meeting had lasted a long time; ‘not so dark as’ compares two times.

sentences.context: Jill had to pinch herself to keep awake, for she knew that if
sentences.simple: Jill had to pinch herself to stay awake, because she knew that if she slept on Glimfeather’s back, she would probably fall off.
sentences.grammar: ‘she knew that if she dozed …, she would probably fall’ is a thought in the past: ‘would’ is the past of ‘will’ and tells what could happen; ‘for’ means ‘because’.

sentences.context: Scrubb had brought the one which had been left out for him
sentences.simple: Scrubb had brought the sword that someone had left out for him in his room at Cair Paravel. But Jill had to be happy with her knife.
sentences.grammar: ‘which had been left out’ is passive past perfect: someone left it earlier; ‘had to be content with’ means she had to accept less.

sentences.context: The others must give an absolute promise that, unless he gave them leave
sentences.simple: The others must promise that, unless he said they could, they would not tell the Gentle Giants that they came from Narnia or that they were looking for Prince Rilian.
sentences.grammar: ‘unless’ means ‘if not’; ‘gave them leave’ means ‘gave them permission’; ‘would not tell’ is the promise, reported in the past.

sentences.context: first of those quarrels which Puddleglum had foretold
sentences.simple: Now they nearly had the first of those quarrels that Puddleglum had said would come. Jill and Scrubb had often snapped at each other before, but this was the first really serious disagreement.
sentences.grammar: ‘had foretold’ (past perfect) says he spoke before it happened; ‘not that … hadn’t been sparring’ says that small fights had happened before.

sentences.context: were absolutely dead set to visit the Gentle Giants
sentences.simple: The children were sick of wind and rain, thin birds cooked over campfires, and hard, cold ground to sleep on. They very much wanted to visit the Gentle Giants.
sentences.grammar: ‘The children, … who were sick of …, were … dead set’: the ‘who’ clause between commas gives the reason; ‘on the other hand’ contrasts them with Puddleglum; ‘dead set to + verb’ means very sure they want to do it.

sentences.context: In order to understand what followed, you must keep on remembering
sentences.simple: To understand what came next, you must keep on remembering how little they could see.
sentences.grammar: ‘In order to + verb’ tells the purpose; ‘what followed’ is a noun clause meaning ‘the things that came next’; ‘keep on + -ing’ means do it again and again.

sentences.context: they could not have heard him even if they had wanted to
sentences.simple: The Marsh-wiggle followed them, still talking. But they were pushing against the wind again, so they could not have heard him, even if they had wanted to.
sentences.grammar: ‘could not have heard … even if they had wanted to’ is about the past: ‘could not have + verb’ says it was impossible, and ‘even if’ + past perfect says that wanting would not change it.

sentences.context: a wind that felt as if it would take your skin off
sentences.simple: Above them was a sky with no sun, covered with clouds heavy with snow. On the ground was a black frost. And a wind blew over it that felt as if it would take your skin off.
sentences.grammar: The sentence is a list of three phrases with no verb until the last; ‘as if it would’ compares the wind to something that is not real.

sentences.context: Puddleglum was dead against any idea of telling the giants their real business
sentences.simple: Puddleglum was very much against any idea of telling the giants why they had really come and just asking to be let out. The children could not tell without his permission, because they had promised.
sentences.grammar: ‘dead against + any idea of + -ing’ means strongly against doing it; ‘because they had promised’ gives an earlier reason.

sentences.context: A few minutes ago when they had been in the kitchen
sentences.simple: A few minutes before, in the kitchen, she had thought that if only they could once get out of the castle, their escape would be almost complete. Now she saw that the most dangerous part was still to come.
sentences.grammar: ‘if only … could’ shows a strong wish; ‘would be’ is a past thought about the future; ‘was still to come’ means it had not happened yet.

sentences.context: Suddenly Puddleglum turned to them, and his face had gone so pale
sentences.simple: Puddleglum suddenly turned to them. His face had gone so pale that you could see the paleness under the natural muddy color of his skin.
sentences.grammar: ‘had gone so pale that …’ shows a result; ‘go’ + adjective means ‘become’, and the past perfect says the change was finished before he turned.

sentences.context: which must have been a long way overhead
sentences.simple: The light was not strong enough to reach the roof of the cave, which must have been very far above them.
sentences.grammar: ‘must have been’ (modal + perfect) is a strong guess about the past: they think it is true but cannot see; the ‘which’ clause adds more about the roof.

sentences.context: (WHICH WAS PIGEON PIE, COLD ham, salad, and cakes) had been brought
sentences.simple: When the meal (pigeon pie, cold ham, salad and cakes) had been brought, and all had pulled their chairs up to the table and begun, the Knight went on.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been brought’ is passive past perfect: the food came first, then the Knight spoke; the words in brackets give extra detail about the meal.

sentences.context: his own sword (which had been taken from him and laid on the table)
sentences.simple: As soon as the prisoner was free, he jumped across the room in one bound, took his own sword and drew it. Someone had taken the sword from him and put it on the table.
sentences.grammar: ‘which had been taken … and laid’ is a passive past perfect ‘which’ clause: it says what had been done to the sword before; the three verbs (crossed, seized, drew) are quick steps.

sentences.context: that they tunnel not a score of feet beneath the very grass
sentences.simple: Her Earthmen have worked day and night to dig a way under it. They have now come so far and so high that their tunnel is less than twenty feet under the grass where the people of that country walk.
sentences.grammar: ‘not a score of feet’ means ‘less than twenty feet’ (a score is twenty); ‘tunnel’ is used as a verb; ‘so far and so high that’ shows a result.

sentences.context: the great serpent which the Witch had become, green as poison
sentences.simple: The Witch had become a great snake, green as poison and as thick as Jill’s waist. Before anyone had time to do anything, it had thrown two or three coils of its horrible body round the Prince’s legs.
sentences.grammar: ‘which the Witch had become’ is a ‘which’ clause in the past perfect: she changed first, then the snake ‘had flung’ its coils; ‘as poison’ and ‘as Jill’s waist’ are comparisons.

sentences.context: whom some call Caspian the Seafarer
sentences.simple: I am Rilian, the King’s son of Narnia. I am the only child of Caspian, Tenth of that name, whom some call Caspian the Seafarer.
sentences.grammar: ‘Tenth of that name’ means the tenth king called Caspian; ‘whom some call …’ is a ‘whom’ clause, where ‘whom’ is the object of ‘call’.

sentences.context: you can put nothing into your make-believe without copying it
sentences.simple: Look: you cannot put anything into your make-believe without copying it from the real world, this world of mine, which is the only world.
sentences.grammar: ‘nothing … without + -ing’ means that every time you put something in, you copy it; the last ‘which’ clause adds a claim about the real world.

sentences.context: They had all, in fact, been hearing the noise but it had begun
sentences.simple: They had all been hearing the noise. But it had started and grown so slowly that they did not know when they first noticed it.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been hearing’ (past perfect continuous) says they heard it for some time before they noticed; ‘so gradually that’ shows a result.

sentences.context: The Witch had locked the door and told the Earthmen not to disturb her
sentences.simple: The Witch had locked the door and told the Earthmen not to disturb her. So for now there was no danger that anyone would stop them.
sentences.grammar: ‘told the Earthmen not to + verb’ is a reported order (a negative command); the past perfect puts it before the time of the story.

sentences.context: would have thought Golg had sent them the wrong way if they
sentences.simple: They would have thought Golg had sent them the wrong way if they had not seen, on the other side of the valley, the lamps going on and up as far as they could see.
sentences.grammar: Third conditional: ‘would have thought … if they had not seen’ is about the past; they did see the lamps, so they did not think they were lost.

sentences.context: and if it had come to swimming, the horses could hardly have won over
sentences.simple: The tide was running up the valley like a fast stream. If it had come to swimming, the horses could hardly have got across.
sentences.grammar: ‘if it had come to swimming’ (past perfect) means ‘if swimming had been needed’, and ‘could hardly have got across’ says it was almost impossible; both talk about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: all sorts of people who had been watching the dance, and whom
sentences.simple: All kinds of people who had been watching the dance, and whom she had not seen at first, came running up.
sentences.grammar: ‘who had been watching’ (past perfect continuous) and ‘whom she had not seen’ are two clauses that tell more about ‘people’ before they came running.

sentences.context: So that when he had persuaded Puddleglum to give him a back
sentences.simple: So when he had talked Puddleglum into giving him a back, and drawn his sword, and put out his head, he had really been doing a very brave thing.
sentences.grammar: ‘when he had persuaded …, and drawn …, and poked out …’ lists three steps in the past perfect; the main clause ‘he had really been doing’ says all of this together was a brave act.

sentences.context: Eustace tackled it just as if he had not had a very large supper
sentences.simple: Breakfast was scrambled eggs and toast. Eustace ate it just as if he had not had a very big supper in the middle of the night.
sentences.grammar: ‘just as if he had not had’ (past perfect) compares to something that was not true: he had eaten a lot; ‘tackled’ means he attacked the food hungrily.

sentences.context: Puddleglum (whose foot was as good as new in three weeks) often pointed out
sentences.simple: Rilian ruled Narnia well, and the land was happy in his days. But Puddleglum (whose foot was as good as new in three weeks) often said that bright mornings are followed by wet afternoons, and that you could not expect good times to last.
sentences.grammar: ‘whose foot’ is a ‘whose’ clause in brackets, meaning ‘the foot of Puddleglum’; ‘though’ contrasts the happy land with Puddleglum’s warnings; ‘as good as new’ is a comparison.

sentences.context: As if you didn’t know perfectly well what weak chests Apes always have
sentences.simple: You act as if you did not know very well that Apes always have weak chests and catch cold very easily.
sentences.grammar: ‘As if you didn’t know’ uses the past tense for something not real: the Ape says Puzzle knows but acts as if he does not; ‘what weak chests Apes always have’ is a noun clause after ‘know’.

sentences.context: And Shift’s voice sounded as if he was just going to burst into tears
sentences.simple: Shift’s voice sounded as if he was about to cry.
sentences.grammar: ‘Sounded as if he was just going to burst into tears’ tells how his voice seemed; ‘be just going to + verb’ means be about to do it; ‘burst into tears’ means suddenly start to cry.

sentences.context: said the Ape (whose mind worked very quickly)
sentences.simple: ‘No, no,’ said the Ape. His mind worked very quickly.
sentences.grammar: ‘(whose mind worked very quickly)’ is a ‘whose’ clause: ‘whose’ means ‘the Ape’s’. The brackets mark extra information in the middle of the sentence.

sentences.context: if the real Aslan, as you call him, meant us to go on with
sentences.simple: I was just going to say that if the real Aslan, as you call him, wanted us to go on with this, he would send us a clap of thunder and a shaking of the earth.
sentences.grammar: ‘If + past (meant), would + verb (send)’ talks about an imagined case, not a real one; ‘was just going to say’ means was about to say; ‘as you call him’ is an extra remark between commas.

sentences.context: and when at last he got somewhere near the thing he was trying to
sentences.simple: When he had come up, he at last got somewhere near the thing he was trying to catch. But it floated away from him until it, too, got under the waterfall and was forced down to the bottom.
sentences.grammar: ‘The thing he was trying to catch’ has no ‘that’: the thing is the object of ‘catch’, so ‘that’ can be left out; ‘was forced down’ is passive (the water did it).

sentences.context: But if someone who had never seen a lion looked at Puzzle in his
sentences.simple: Someone who had never seen a lion might think Puzzle in his lion-skin was a lion. This could happen if he did not come too close, if the light was not too good, and if Puzzle did not bray or make any noise with his hoofs.
sentences.grammar: ‘Someone who had never seen a lion’ is a ‘who’ clause in the past perfect; ‘might mistake X for Y’ means might wrongly think X is Y; each ‘if + didn’t ...’ is one condition that must be true.

sentences.context: He was so old that no one could remember when he had first come
sentences.simple: He was so old that no one could remember when he had first come to live in those parts. He was the cleverest, ugliest, most wrinkled Ape you can imagine.
sentences.grammar: ‘So old that’ shows a result; ‘had first come’ (past perfect) is a time before ‘could remember’; ‘the cleverest, ugliest, most wrinkled’ are superlatives (the most of all).

sentences.context: Roonwit had just raised his hand and was leaning forward
sentences.simple: Roonwit had just lifted his hand and was leaning forward to say something very seriously to the King. Then all three of them turned their heads to listen to a wailing sound that was quickly coming nearer.
